Guidance: Military low flying: air weapons ranges activity
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
12:43:58 BST
20:43:58 KST

Military low flying: air weapons ranges activity
Notification of extended operating hours and low flying activities for UK air weapons ranges: Donna Nook, Holbeach, Pembrey Sands, Tain and Cape Wrath.
Documents
Details
The above activity is planned range use but in exceptional circumstances there may be additional activity at short notice.
The MOD is aware of the disturbance that can be caused to local residents by activity at the UK Air Weapons Ranges (AWR). Notification of the pre-planned extended operating hours will be published at the earliest opportunity.
It should be noted that when an AWR is closed, the segregated airspace above it no longer has Danger Area status and reverts to Class G airspace, meaning that it becomes freely available to all airspace users (both civilian and military).
The MOD currently uses 5 AWRs for essential operational training:
- Donna Nook and Holbeach in Lincolnshire
- Pembrey Sands in Carmarthenshire
- Tain in Ross-shire
- Cape Wrath in Sutherland.

Horsing around: How Trump's AI George Washington image has symbolically backfired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:41:41 UTC
20:41:41 KST

Donald Trump's latest AI-generated image, depicting him horse riding alongside George Washington, has backfired as many have pointed out the symbolic blunder of him riding a black horse in the current climate...
Donald Trump is no stranger to bulk posting AI-generated imagery as part of what has been referred to as “memetic warfare” - a tactic which sees him and his administration flood the zone when it comes to AI slop in order to appeal to his base and beyond.
While this social media strategy isn't new, one recently shared image has once again shown that the use of AI can be detrimental when it comes to conveying the proper message. Specifically, how the AI images he posts frequently backfire due to a lack of understanding when it comes to cultural references.
His recent cultural blunder is a symbolic one, which comes with an image he posted yesterday. It sees Trump horse riding with Founding Father and first president of the United States, George Washington.
The self-aggrandising image sees Washington riding a white horse, while Trump is on a black stallion.
While it's not the first time that Trump has hijacked the figure of George Washington, having posted a series of AI images of himself showing Washington around the new White House ballroom, it didn't take long for many to point out the symbolically charged equine error on show.
The cultural connotations of the black horse are numerous, and usually negative. In Henry Fuseli's 1781 masterpiece 'The Nightmare', the ghostly dark horse is a sleep paralysis demon and the embodiment of repressed dread.
In modern symbolism, the black horse can reflect hidden desires and dark secrets, but generally belongs to a series of images mirroring what psychologist Carl Jung called "the shadow self", which includes repressed anger and shame.
Then comes the Biblical reading, as the black horse is a known reference within apocalyptic contexts. The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse in the Book of Revelation all ride different coloured horses. The white horse is pestilence; the red horse represents war; the pale horse is death; and the black horse is famine, representing food scarcity and economic hardship.
Considering Trump's image comes at a time when the price of gas, food and other essentials have soared due to the Iran war, which has now entered its sixth month, the image of him riding a black horse feels accidentally apt - what some have referred to as a "catastrophic self-own".
Social media users pointed out that Trump's handling of the ongoing US affordability crisis is unfortunately reflected in this symbolically loaded image, while others have made references to pop culture and films, with one X user noting: “Does Trump know that bad guys ride the black horse?”
Much like the red lightsaber SNAFU or the irony of portraying himself as Superman or using Spider-Man references, the misused cultural connotations have once again revealed a certain level of cultural illiteracy...
It's not the only black and white slip-up that has sparked alarm this weekend...
Trump posted a black and white 2028 image on Truth Social, which has been perceived as yet another inidication that he will be persuing a third term and is considering being president in 2028 - despite this being unconstitutional due to a two-term limit.
The image, posted with the caption “We are going to win” has reminded people of how Trump began selling red 2028 caps last year.
“I don’t think he’s planning on leaving,” said one X user, while another commented: “America needs to brace for chaos in 2028’s elections. NOT GOOD”.

Chinese national jailed over B-2 base photography
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
12:40:28 BST
20:40:28 KST

A Chinese national has been jailed for six months after returning to Whiteman Air Force Base and photographing the sensitive B-2 bomber installation despite an earlier warning, according to the US Air Force.
A Chinese national has been sentenced to six months in federal custody after repeatedly photographing Whiteman Air Force Base, home of the US Air Force’s B-2 Spirit stealth bomber fleet, the UK Defence Journal understands.
According to a US Air Force news update, Qilin Wu returned to the Missouri installation after previously being warned not to photograph the base. Investigators said his conduct included taking images not only of aircraft but also of the installation’s perimeter and infrastructure, eventually leading to an investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, a guilty plea and sentencing.
The case was brought using Section 795 of Title 18 of the US Code together with Executive Order 10104, a 76-year-old measure signed by President Harry Truman. The legislation prohibits unauthorised photographs, sketches, maps and other visual representations of designated military installations, aircraft, weapons and equipment where protection from general dissemination is required. US Air Force officials presented the prosecution as an example of an older legal framework being applied to contemporary security concerns around sensitive military sites.
Colonel David Bethel, commander of AFOSI Region 8, said, as quoted in the news update: “For our Special Agents, this isn’t about a single case. It’s about recognizing that the operating environment has changed.” Bethel said investigators increasingly had to consider activity around military installations in the United States that might not initially present as an obvious security threat. He added: “When someone gathers information around a sensitive military installation, AFOSI has the tools to hold them accountable.”
The incident began on 2 December 2025, when personnel from the 509th Security Forces Squadron responded to a report concerning a suspicious minivan close to the perimeter of Whiteman Air Force Base. Wu, who was driving a vehicle with Massachusetts licence plates, told personnel that he had travelled there to observe the B-2. Investigators said the subsequent concern arose from his return after being warned and the range of subjects photographed around the base.
A senior AFOSI official involved in the investigation said, as quoted in the same news update: “What made this different was the pattern of behavior.” The Air Force said Wu later admitted photographing aircraft and installations at other US military bases, including locations in Florida and Virginia. The published account does not state that he was convicted of espionage, instead describing the offence in terms of unauthorised photography of protected military property.
Following sentencing, Wu was remanded to the US Marshals Service. The U.S. Air Force said he was subsequently processed on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainer and is expected to be deported to China.
Whiteman Air Force Base is the principal operating base for the B-2 Spirit, one of the United States’ most sensitive strategic bomber platforms.
The installation is home to the 509th Bomb Wing and forms part of the country’s nuclear and conventional long-range strike capability, making activity around its perimeter a particular counter-intelligence and force-protection concern.
AFOSI said it would continue to investigate suspected unauthorised photography around protected installations and equipment, with individual cases assessed according to their circumstances. Bethel said the Whiteman investigation demonstrated the role of installation security personnel and federal investigators in identifying potentially concerning activity before it develops further, adding: “Det. 811’s work delivered strategic deterrence. This case reflects AFOSI’s professionalism, integration and operational discipline required to defend our installations in an increasingly complex threat environment.”

Unknown

Dilara Hamit
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
Marvel blockbuster ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ has surpassed $2 billion in worldwide ticket sales after just three weekends in theaters, becoming only the eighth film in history to reach the milestone.
The film has grossed approximately $2.022 billion globally, including $785.8 million in North America and $1.236 billion from international markets, according to box-office tracking data.
The performance makes it the second-fastest film to cross the $2 billion mark, behind ‘Avengers: Endgame,’ which reached the milestone in 11 days.
‘Brand New Day’ had earlier become the second-fastest film to earn $1 billion worldwide, reaching that mark within its first week of release.
The latest installment is Tom Holland’s fourth standalone film as Peter Parker and has surpassed 2021’s ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home,’ which grossed about $1.92 billion, to become the highest-grossing Spider-Man film and Sony Pictures release.
The film currently ranks seventh on the all-time worldwide box-office chart, without adjusting for inflation. It has overtaken the Chinese animated film ‘Ne Zha 2,’ which grossed just over $2 billion, and is closing in on ‘Avengers: Infinity War’ and ‘Star Wars: The Force Awakens.’
The movie also remained atop the North American box office for a third consecutive weekend, adding an estimated $70 million domestically.
‘Brand New Day’ joins ‘Avatar’, ‘Avengers: Endgame,’ ‘Avatar: The Way of Water’, ‘Titanic,’ ‘Star Wars: The Force Awakens’, ‘Avengers: Infinity War’ and ‘Ne Zha 2’ as the only films to have surpassed $2 billion at the worldwide box office.

Türkiye's budget deficit widens nearly 16-fold in July as interest payments surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:40:05 CST
20:40:05 KST

ANKARA, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye's central government budget deficit surged 1,484.6 percent year on year to 378.1 billion Turkish liras (about 7.9 billion U.S. dollars) in July from 23.9 billion liras a year earlier, according to data released Monday by the Turkish ministry of treasury and finance.
The sharp deterioration was largely attributed to a significant increase in interest payments. Interest expenditure more than doubled year on year, rising 142.8 percent to 326.8 billion liras in July.
Central government budget spending increased 59.8 percent year on year to 1.8 trillion liras, while budget revenues rose 28.8 percent to 1.4 trillion liras. Tax revenues increased 30 percent year on year to 1.2 trillion liras, while income-tax revenue rose 47.9 percent to 432 billion liras.
However, corporate tax revenue fell sharply by 69.8 percent year on year to 3.6 billion liras, weighing on overall tax collection.
The central government budget deficit reached 1.3 trillion liras during the January-July period, compared with 1 trillion liras in the same period of 2025.
Despite the wider overall deficit, the primary balance remained in surplus at 470.1 billion liras, up from 241.7 billion liras a year earlier, official data showed. ■

China publishes selected works of Jiang Zemin on foreign policy

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:40:01 CST
20:40:01 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- A collection of selected works by late Chinese leader Jiang Zemin on foreign policy has been published.
The book, jointly compiled by the Institute of Party History and Literature of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, contains 115 reports, speeches, remarks, letters, responses to questions and other documents on foreign policy by Jiang from July 1989 to July 2003. Some of the works were made public for the first time.
The publication came as China held a grand gathering to commemorate Jiang's birth centenary on Monday.
Born in August 1926, Jiang was elected general secretary of the CPC Central Committee in 1989. He was the core of the third generation of the Party's central collective leadership and the principal founder of the Theory of Three Represents. In 2022, Jiang passed away at the age of 96.
The collection reflects Jiang's important thinking and outstanding contributions to the theory and practice of China's diplomacy of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The book is now available nationwide. ■

DR Congo Ebola outbreak deadliest ever in country's history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:40:00 UTC
20:40:00 KST

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has become the country’s deadliest, killing over 2,300 people in three months, officials said Monday.
The United Nations says the Ebola outbreak "is the fastest growing on record" and is killing a victim every 30 minutes in the DRC.
No specific vaccine or treatment exists for the Bundibugyo strain behind the current surge of Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a hemorrhagic fever.
Declared on May 15, the DRC's 17th Ebola outbreak is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks by that point.
It has hit regions in the north and east where the presence of the state is weak, health infrastructure is largely lacking and myriad armed groups have roamed for decades.
A 2018-2020 outbreak in the DRC, previously considered the country's deadliest, killed 2,299 people out of 3,381 confirmed cases, according to World Health Organization (WHO) figures based on Congolese data.
In its latest toll on Monday, the Congolese authorities said that 2,325 people had died in the current outbreak, from 4,945 confirmed cases.
The deadliest Ebola outbreak ever hit West Africa in 2013-2016, killing more than 11,300 people, mainly in Liberia, Sierra Leone and Guinea.
The WHO last week said it hoped to reverse the spread of the disease in the DRC within three months.
The latest outbreak began in the conflict-scarred northeastern province of Ituri and has since spread to five other provinces in the sprawling central African country of more than 100 million people.
In Bunia, the capital of Ituri province where most of the cases have been recorded, measures against the disease remain scarcely visible.
The town hall ordered traders to install hand-washing facilities in front of their shops, but customers continue to flock to the markets while paying little heed to protective measures, an AFP correspondent saw.
"Community engagement in the response is still far too weak," Mohamed Janabi, WHO regional director for Africa, said.
More than 70% of people die in the community and not in health centers, he added.
"People prefer to be treated at home, thinking it is a case of poisoning or some other illness," said Jean-Paul Malo Lotsima, a civil society official in the Djugu area of Ituri.
"It's often at the last minute, when the family realises that the situation is getting worse, that patients are taken to hospital. And sometimes, they die on the way," he added.
Flavier Ngurima, who lives in Nizi, one of the hotspots of the outbreak in Ituri, said his brother died before reaching the treatment centre.
"We had called on a nurse from the family to treat him at home because the patient and the family members were afraid to go to the ETC (treatment centre)," he said.
"They said that over there, a lot of people die."
Access to affected communities is also hampered by armed groups active in some of the regions hit by the outbreak, aid groups say.
North Kivu and South Kivu are split by the front lines between the Congolese army and the anti-government M23 armed group, backed by Rwanda, which has seized vast swathes of territory.
Despite efforts by international organizations, the response has faced criticism for being slow and unorganized.
Local staff, including nurses and those in charge of safe burials, have gone on strike or demonstrated in several hospitals in Ituri in recent weeks to demand payment of bonuses.
The International Council of Nurses on Friday urged the DRC's authorities to provide proper pay and protection for health care workers fighting the outbreak.
Several vaccines are being tested against the current strain of Ebola.

Laos shifts to digital ID system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:39:50 CST
20:39:50 KST

VIENTIANE, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- Laos' Ministry of Public Security has officially launched the LAeID application nationwide and announced that old-style identity cards, including the white and green cards, will no longer be accepted for official transactions.
The move is part of Laos' broader digital transformation efforts, aimed at replacing the traditional census registration system with a modern electronic system. LAeID is designed to facilitate the management, verification and use of information contained in the national citizen database and identity card system, Lao News Agency reported on Monday.
The ministry has called on government ministries and agencies, local authorities, civil servants, businesses, and citizens nationwide to register and keep their personal information up to date through the LAeID application.
Electronic records stored through the system may serve as official references for employment-related matters and various transactions, reducing the need for traditional paper-based census registration books.
The ministry has urged all relevant organizations and individuals to cooperate with the transition to the electronic identity system and comply with the new requirements.
The Lao government reaffirmed its commitment to advancing digital transformation as a key driver of national development, continuing efforts to enhance e-government services, develop a digitally skilled workforce, and promote overall digital growth. ■

Explainer: Why U.S. finds itself in stalemate as 60-day peace deadline expires
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:39:40 CST
20:39:40 KST

TEHRAN/WASHINGTON, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- The 60-day window established under the June 18 peace memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Iran and the United States expires on Monday, marking a critical moment for an agreement that was meant to create space for diplomacy and de-escalation.
Yet as the deadline arrives, Washington finds itself increasingly trapped in a stalemate, unable to secure a military victory or revive diplomacy.
DIRECT TALKS IN LIMBO
On June 18, Iran and the United States signed the MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts, including Lebanon.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within a 60-day period, ending on Monday, to reach a final agreement. However, the fate of the talks has been hanging in the balance amid continued escalations between the two countries since the signing of the document.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi has said that Iran has yet to decide on resuming negotiations with the United States, the state-run IRIB news agency reported Saturday.
Araghchi stressed that the United States has "violated" the MoU and that clashes have resumed.
On July 7 and 8, U.S. forces launched strikes against Iran for two consecutive days, citing the attacks as a response to Iranian attacks on commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz. In retaliation, Iran launched missile and drone attacks against U.S. facilities in countries including Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and Jordan. The United States subsequently launched another sustained campaign of strikes beginning July 11, carrying out attacks on Iran for 13 consecutive nights through July 23, according to the U.S. Central Command.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on July 8, during the NATO summit, that the MoU with Iran "is over," and that he no longer wanted to deal with Iran. In a follow-up interview on July 13, Trump claimed the agreement was "built to test" Iran, stating, "They didn't honor the test." Although U.S. officials have since made few public references to the peace MoU, Trump has repeatedly said that talks with Iran were underway. Tehran, however, has repeatedly denied that any negotiations were being held or planned, leaving the resumption of direct talks between the two sides in limbo.
SANCTIONS AND THREATS
Washington has continued to escalate pressure on Tehran through financial sanctions and threats of further military action.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday that Washington is stepping up a financial campaign against Tehran that began after Trump reinstated his "maximum pressure" policy last year and intensified following the launch of military operations against Iran in February.
"We are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country," Bessent said in an interview, adding that the Treasury Department has targeted Iranian "bank accounts, crypto wallets, assets around the world, cutting off payments into both the leadership in the regime and the government itself."
The Treasury Department would pursue a combination of economic isolation and a continued blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Bessent said.
Also in recent weeks, Trump has repeatedly threatened to resume major combat operations against Iran with "bigger than ever before" strikes. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the United States "is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II."
Yet in early August, Trump said that he had agreed to hold off fresh attacks at the request of Iran and other Middle Eastern countries.
The decision came amid growing concerns over U.S. ammunition stockpiles. Media reported that the U.S. military had exhausted nearly 80 percent of the interceptors for a key missile defense system during the war, as military commanders warned that the army's munitions stockpile was "dangerously low."
Analysts noted that the glaring contrast between Washington's aggressive rhetoric and its sudden military pause fully exposes the reality that the United States is struggling to sustain a high-intensity war of attrition.
HORMUZ STANDOFF
So far, the United States and Iran have been locked in a standoff over the control and ownership of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran continued to pursue diplomatic channels over the waterway. Araghchi noted in an interview Saturday that messages are being exchanged between Iran and the United States through mediators, namely Qatar and Pakistan, "but this does not mean negotiations at all."
At the same time, Iran and Oman are negotiating a new route for the safe passage of vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi said. "And we are currently designing a temporary route, which will turn into a permanent one in the next stages."
"We may reach a conclusion soon," he added. However, he said that the reopening of the strait hinges on the fulfillment of other conditions, "to which the United States must be committed."
Washington, meanwhile, has taken an increasingly assertive position over the Strait of Hormuz. Trump said Friday that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a U.S. territory.
"After we finish defeating Iran -- which is being very badly defeated -- pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," he said during a rally in New York.
The remarks reinforced statements Trump made Wednesday, when he claimed that the United States has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz and will "keep it."
Trump said on Truth Social that the U.S. naval blockade of the waterway had been described as a "wall of steel," adding that Iran lacked the capability to challenge it.
In response, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi posted on X that "The Strait of Hormuz can be captured neither with a tweet and aircraft carriers nor by issuing orders and a stump speech. Iran is neither afraid of threats nor intimidated by displays of power."
"This strait will only be closed and opened under Iran's command," he added.
According to the official IRNA news agency, Iran's Army Chief Amir Hatami on Sunday issued a stern warning against any military mischief by the United States, adding that the Americans have effectively been expelled from the region and would no longer be allowed to enter the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman or the Strait of Hormuz. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's 70 major cities generally saw narrowed year-on-year home price drops in July, adding to signs of stabilization of the property market, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Monday.
In the four first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, new home prices fell 1.1 percent year on year last month, compared with a 1.3-percent drop in June, while the decline in second-hand home prices narrowed from 4.9 percent to 3.7 percent in July.
In other cities, year-on-year declines of home prices also narrowed slightly in July, except new home prices in third-tier cities, where the decline was unchanged from June.
On a month-on-month basis, home prices in first-tier cities generally rose, while those in second- and third-tier cities went down. Across the 70 cities, 23 recorded increases or no change in new home prices, two more than in June, while the figure for second-hand homes was eight, two fewer than the previous month.
The NBS releases a monthly home price report tracking market changes in 70 major cities, including four first-tier cities, 31 second-tier cities and 35 third-tier cities.
More signs emerging this year suggest the property market has remained broadly stable with confidence and expectations gradually improving.
At a meeting on economic work held by the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee at the end of last month, policymakers called for continued efforts to stabilize the property market.
Experts said the policy direction remains clear, with local governments expected to make better use of policy tools tailored to local conditions to meet housing demand.
Yu Xiaofen, a researcher at Zhejiang University of Technology in east China, called for faster progress in developing a new model for the property sector, as well as improving long-term mechanisms to promote the stable and healthy development of the market. ■

Researchers in Australia grow "mini guts" to study inflammatory bowel disease
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:39:28 CST
20:39:28 KST

MELBOURNE, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have grown live models of pediatric patients' digestive systems, or "mini guts," to investigate solutions for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Using live tissue and bacteria from the intestine to create miniature 3D "organoid" models, researchers have been able to test how and where the specific bacteria in a patient's digestive system can affect tissue and cause inflammation, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's Monash University.
The study, published in Scientific Reports, is the first to develop an organoid model incorporating both the intestinal lining and its bacteria, and pioneers the technology to inject bacteria into the intestinal organoids to study their impact on inflammation, the statement said.
The gut microbiome is unique to each person, which means an IBD treatment that works for one person may not work for another. The "mini guts" could help move IBD treatment beyond a "one-size-fits-all" approach, said lead researcher Professor Helen Abud from the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.
"By creating living replicas of a patient's intestinal lining, we can observe how this critical barrier protects the body from harmful gut contents, and how it heals or breaks down when exposed to different bacteria," Abud said.
Senior researcher Adjunct Associate Professor Edward Giles at Monash University and the Hudson Institute of Medical Research said the method provides a way to test whether healing of the intestinal barrier can be promoted or even find "protective" bacteria that could become treatments themselves.
First author Dr Eva Chan at the Hudson Institute of Medical Research said building a biobank of matched organoids and bacterial collections from individual patients could lay the groundwork for testing and tailoring interventions in the lab before they reach patients. ■

Feature: In Lebanon's ruins, a woman becomes the keeper of the dead
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:39:19 CST
20:39:19 KST

BEIRUT, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- In a long black robe and headscarf, Maryam Aqil moves through Nabatieh's shattered streets, buildings scarred by shelling, roads still torn open by war.
To many, she looks like any local woman walking through her hometown, a southern Lebanese city. But each corner pulls her back to war, when she took on one of its heaviest burdens: washing the bodies of airstrike victims, gathering their remains, and laying them to rest.
Aqil, in her sixties, stayed in Nabatieh when many others left. She told Xinhua she was not seeking an extraordinary role, but felt that victims' families needed someone to honor their dead and prepare them for their final farewell.
"Often, I was alone as there was no one else who could do this task." Aqil said.
She still remembers the relentless shelling and the ambulances and Red Cross vans wailing toward her, ferrying victims the strikes claimed without mercy: the old, women, and children.
The vivid account unfolds against an Israeli war that has inflicted extensive human losses in Lebanon: 4,346 dead and 12,301 wounded since March 2, according to the latest health ministry figures.
The task left a profound impact on Aqil.
"No human being can see human remains without being affected. And what stayed with me most were the children whose bodies were torn apart through no fault of their own. I suffered greatly," she said.
Aqil herself lost her cousin in an airstrike. Pointing to places around her, she recalled the dangers she faced.
"Here, a house was hit by shelling. Another was destroyed. There was a street where families disappeared, and every corner witnessed an incident that left behind the memory of someone I knew."
"There was only a thin line between life and death," she said.
Despite the pain of seeing charred, torn bodies, Aqil regarded her work as a solemn responsibility.
"The families were waiting for their loved ones, and I considered that my duty. People needed someone to stand beside them," she said.
Usually, she would use camphor and traditional Arabic soap, obtained from health centers, to wash the bodies.
"Despite all the difficulties, I never thought of leaving," Aqil said.
Amid the fragile calm in Nabatieh and nearby villages, Aqil walks streets that remember the bombs.
"Time may erase some details, but places do not forget. Here, an airstrike took place; there, a family lost one of its members; and somewhere else, I carried the remains of someone who was killed," she said. "These places have become part of my memory." ■

Feature: China's young voices join global conversation on green shipping
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
19:39:18 CST
20:39:18 KST

LONDON, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- Inside the main building of University College London, a group of young Chinese and British students gathered for an international exchange on one of the most pressing challenges facing the maritime industry: how to make shipping greener.
One after another, students from China's Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) and Britain's University College London took the floor, sharing research and debating practical solutions for the shipping industry's transition to a low-carbon future.
Outside, London was enduring intense summer heat, which gave the discussion an added sense of urgency.
What fuels should ships use? How can ports efficiently supply cleaner fuels? Can promising technologies move beyond laboratories and research papers into real-world operations? These were not merely theoretical questions for the students.
Some presented research into autonomous systems operating in complex waters, while others explored ways to improve the efficiency of methanol bunkering at ports. One group shared research on the development and operation of China's electric vessels.
The exchange was part of a field research project organized by SJTU under its Global Challenge Program.
During the visit in London last week, SJTU students met with representatives of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS), Lloyd's Register, and the Royal Institute of Navigation, discussing ship technologies, green fuels, and international maritime regulations.
At the IACS, the students did not hesitate to ask tricky questions: What are the biggest obstacles to achieving net-zero emissions in global shipping? How can university research be translated more effectively into industrial applications?
The answers pointed to a challenge that extends well beyond technological innovation. Universities, industry, and international organizations need to work more closely together, with researchers working alongside classification societies, shipowners, shipyards and industry bodies to turn academic findings into technical recommendations, and eventually international proposals.
For Yue Mingyuan, a SJTU doctoral student, that message resonated deeply.
Yue previously interned at the IMO and now focuses on the application of green energy in ports and ships, including shore power and methanol as alternative energy sources.
"Companies bring us real problems. We use models and algorithms to find solutions, and then those solutions have to be tested in real-world settings," Yue said. "Only then do we have a real chance of producing something that can actually be used."
That emphasis on practical application was echoed by Robert Ashdown, IACS secretary general, who described the students' visit as constructive and meaningful in terms of academic research, talent development and the transformation of the shipping industry.
The IACS looks forward to deepening its cooperation with SJTU, Ashdown said.
James Frew, advisory director of Lloyd's Register, also expressed hope for closer cooperation with SJTU, saying that more joint achievements could help bring China's experience in green shipping to Europe and the wider world.
For the students, the significance of the trip went beyond individual research projects.
Whether sitting in on meetings at the IMO or exchanging views with international maritime professionals, they were gaining a first-hand understanding of how the global shipping industry works, and how China's experience is increasingly becoming part of conversations about international maritime rules and the future of the sector.
"The most important part of the experience was giving students the opportunity to connect classroom knowledge with the realities of international shipping," said Hu Hao, assistant to the SJTU president and a professor at its School of Ocean and Civil Engineering.
The purpose of exchanges like this, Hu said, is twofold: to give the world a better understanding of China's experience in the maritime sector, while helping young people recognize that Chinese ideas, technologies and practices are becoming an increasingly important part of international dialogue.
As a global center for maritime regulation, shipping finance and insurance, and the operations of multinational companies, London offers a unique vantage point to observe the evolution of global shipping governance and the industry's green transition.
Arsenio Dominguez, IMO secretary-general, said that China has shared extensive practical experience with the IMO in areas including port operations, seafarer education and training, and ship design and construction.
From technical challenges aboard ships to alternative fuels at ports and debates over international rules, the young Chinese students in London were witnessing a maritime industry in the midst of profound change.
They were not simply observing that transformation, but beginning to find their own place within it -- bringing their research, experience, and questions to the international stage, allowing the global conversation on green shipping to hear young voices from China. ■

Dutch coal-fired power plants see highest output in years: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:37:46 UTC
20:37:46 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
Coal-fired power plants in the Netherlands are generating electricity at their highest levels in years, Dutch broadcaster NOS reported Monday.
Figures from the Netherlands’ National Energy Dashboard show that coal-fired plants have already generated more electricity this year than during all of 2024, NOS reported, citing financial daily Het Financieele Dagblad (FD).
Output through Aug. 14 remains below the level recorded for all of 2025, but the report said that figure is also likely to be surpassed.
Coal-fired power plants last operated at similarly high levels during the 2022 gas crisis, when Russia’s war on Ukraine sent gas prices soaring.
A similar situation has emerged amid the war in Iran, despite a higher CO2 levy on the use of coal, the report said.
The increased coal-fired generation was attributed mainly to high energy prices and a sharp rise in electricity demand from neighboring Belgium.
“Coal-fired power plants are also stepping in because demand for electricity from abroad has increased,” said Martien Visser, emeritus lecturer in energy transition at Hanze University of Applied Sciences in Groningen.
“We are exporting a lot of electricity abroad,” Visser added.
Belgium had to import much of its electricity during the first half of the year as two major nuclear power plants underwent maintenance, according to the report.
Visser said the increased use of coal-fired power plants was not necessarily bad news, citing European agreements on overall emissions under which higher emissions in one country would have to be offset by lower emissions elsewhere.
He also argued that greater reliance on coal-fired plants was not only a necessity but could also provide an opportunity to conserve natural gas.
“By using coal-fired power plants, we save 60 million cubic meters of gas per week. We can use that to replenish our gas reserves,” Visser added.

With shadow cabinet backing the bill, it is expected to pass. However, Liberal sources have told the ABC some in the party are considering crossing the floor because they believe the laws still will not be strong enough.
Communications Minister Anika Wells used a speech in parliament, before the deal was finalised, to signal Labor was poised to move on so-called gambling inducements and online ads, after criticism its bill did not go far enough.
"It is expected that the government's reforms will respond to these concerns by introducing new restrictions on inducement-based marketing and establishing the wagering advertising opt-out register, which will provide Australians with a one-stop shop to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms," she said.
In addition to TV and radio restrictions, the government's current draft bill creates a "triple lock" system that would require social media, streaming and other online platforms only show gambling ads to logged-in users verified as over 18.
The platforms would also have to give every adult the ability to opt out, a system criticised by the Greens and Coalition as too onerous for Australians, who would have to do this manually for every online account.
Some of the naysayers had advocated for an opt-in system instead, but as the ABC revealed, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was not prepared to entertain such a large change.
Instead, the compromise position put forward by the Coalition was to create a single register for Australians to indicate their wish to opt out of gambling ads.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Mr Albanese met several times to negotiate the gambling laws, which Labor is seeking to pass by the end of this week.
Proposed opt-out register questioned by industry
The opt-out register would be established by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), with people able to request their various online accounts be blocked from viewing gambling advertising.
It is understood the plan would be for people to provide information such as their email address linked to the platform they are seeking to opt out of ads on.
The register is not expected to be in place immediately from January 1, when the broader ad restrictions are due to take effect.
Its principle would be similar to the existing "do not call" register, which is a secure government database where Australians can opt out of receiving unsolicited telemarketing calls.
But tonight, multiple sources in the wagering and tech industry immediately questioned how this approach would be feasible, given the complexity and breadth of online platforms.
There were also concerns raised about who would pay for the register and how.
Currently, the federal government's wagering self-exclusion register, Betstop, is funded by gambling companies, who contribute an amount effectively based on a ratio of their market share.
But one wagering source said companies did not expect to pay for the administration of a second register for advertising.
A tech industry source said an opt-out system made available to individuals was "very different" compared to requiring platforms to proactively comply with a centralised register.
Targeted restriction of inducements proposed
Rather than a broader crackdown on gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, amendments to the legislation are aimed at protecting vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.
It is understood this would include creating a cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending inducements to any new accounts or to people who have recently removed themselves from Betstop.
The proposed amendments are also expected to crack down on VIP account managers at wagering companies earning commissions based on their clients' spending.
The ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp have already stopped this practice.
Discussions are also ongoing about an independent review mechanism to assess the effectiveness of the laws in the future.
Last week, Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament to back this idea.
"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more,"
Senate inquiry report makes one recommendation
A report released tonight, following a short two-day inquiry into the government's gambling legislation earlier this month, recommended the bills be passed.
The single recommendation from the government-authored report was described as "not surprising, but tragic" by independent ACT senator David Pocock.
"We heard from basically everyone other than the gambling companies who said this bill does not protect children, it doesn't break the link between sport and gambling companies," he told the ABC.
Senator Pocock wrote a dissenting report from the inquiry, calling on the government to implement the original recommendations put forward in the You Win Some, You Lose More report by late Labor MP Peta Murphy.
This included a full ban on gambling ads being phased in over three years, an immediate ban on gambling inducements, and the establishment of a single national online gambling regulator.
Senator Pocock also provided fallback amendments to strengthen Labor's existing bill, including extending the gambling ad ban during live sport to after 8:30pm, and replacing the online opt-out "triple lock" system with an opt-in model.
In his report, Senator Pocock referenced evidence given to the inquiry by the family of a 24-year-old man with a severe gambling addiction who died by suicide.
The witnesses told the Senate committee there were "no words to describe this pain", and the family now "lives a half life".
The Greens also provided a dissenting report, arguing the minor party would not support the bill in its current form.
Greens communications spokeswoman Senator Sarah Hanson-Young called for a complete ban on all online gambling ads, the establishment of a national regulator and an end to inducements.
She also recommended the introduction of separate legislation requiring gambling companies to forfeit money they received that was the proceeds of crime.
That was based on evidence heard by the inquiry that wagering companies could retain money gambled by customers who obtained it through criminal offending.

Fuel sale restrictions spread again to nearly all of Russia – Reuters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17

20:36:00 KST

Fuel sale restrictions spread again to nearly all of Russia – Reuters
A new wave of fuel shortages that began in early August has already spread to nearly all of Russia.
Source: Reuters
Details: Petrol was once again unavailable at some filling stations in Moscow Oblast on the morning of 17 August, although diesel was available at almost all petrol stations.
The fuel crisis, which began gaining momentum in May and spread to nearly all Russian regions by July, was caused by seasonal growth in demand and the shutdown of several oil refineries following drone attacks.
By the end of July, the situation had stabilised and restrictions were lifted or significantly eased in some regions. However, the respite did not last long.
A new wave of drone attacks on oil refineries in late July and early August triggered another round of restrictions.
Most Russian regions are now seeing severe restrictions on fuel sales, while partial restrictions are in place in 16 regions.
The Russian government said the most difficult fuel supply situation was in Orenburg, Lipetsk, Oryol and Tver oblasts, Krasnodar Krai, Zabaykalsky Krai, Primorsky Krai and Krasnoyarsk Krai, as well as in Tuvan Autonomous Oblast and Khakas Autonomous Oblast.
Background:
- In early August, a new wave of the fuel crisis appeared to have hit Russia, judging by reports from the regions, amid Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries.
- In late July, the Russian government previously extended its ban on petrol exports until 31 January 2027 and on diesel exports until 31 August 2026.

Attacks on Ukrainian ports on the Danube have peaked - Romania’s Ministry of Defense
Kyiv • UNN
Romania’s acting defense minister said that more than 100 Russian drones had attacked Ukrainian ports on the Danube, with their debris washing up on the Romanian shore. He emphasized that the war has indirect consequences for Romania, but that the level of risk has not increased.
The increase in the number of Russian drones entering Romanian airspace is a direct consequence of the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports on the Danube. Romania’s acting defense minister, Radu Miruță, said this in an interview with Digi24, reports UNN.
Details
"The incidents whose indirect consequences we are observing on the border with Romania are directly proportional to the increase in the number of incidents occurring in Ukraine in recent days. The number of attacks on Ukrainian ports on the Danube has reached its highest level in recent times. On the Ministry of Defense’s radars near Romanian airspace, but already over Ukrainian territory, we detected more than 100 drones—more than 100 one-way devices that formed swarms and attacked Ukrainian ports on the Danube seven times in recent days with a large number of drones," Miruță said.
He noted that the Ukrainian army shot down most of these drones, but their destruction several dozen meters from Romanian airspace resulted in the waters of the Danube and sea waves carrying the debris ashore in Romania on the second, third, or fourth day.
"The largest amount of debris was washed ashore this weekend. We know about it; the war is obviously real. I believe it is very important that Romanians no longer fall under the influence of this pro-Russian propaganda, which is trying to shape public opinion as though this war does not exist. I am telling you this as the defense minister who sees the military data, who sees the consequences of this war, who sees information that cannot be made public because it is classified—this war exists, and this war has indirect consequences for Romania. At present, there are no signs that the level of risk to Romania has increased," Miruță added.

Voyager expands solid rocket motor manufacturing in Colorado
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:35:09 UTC
20:35:09 KST

- Voyager Technologies said U.S. solid rocket motor production is not keeping pace with Department of War demand and detailed its scale-up plans.
- The company's Voyager American Defense Complex, a 150,000-square-foot facility in Pueblo, Colorado, is expected to become operational later in 2026.
Voyager Technologies said domestic production of tactical solid rocket motors is not keeping pace with Department of War demand, and detailed how the company is scaling manufacturing to close that gap.
Solid rocket motors combine fuel and oxidizer in a pressure vessel with a single nozzle exit point, producing thrust as soon as they are ignited. The motors can be manufactured, stored and remain ready for use for 10 to 20 years, according to Voyager, a characteristic the company said makes them useful for stockpiling ahead of need.
“We have a unique integration of expertise across Voyager, bringing together propulsion and defense systems that can deliver on the nation’s most demanding programs,” said Matt Magaña, president, Space, Defense and National Security, Voyager. “At the same time, our commercial approach keeps us agile. We’re operating under decades of mission-proven experience, while still innovating and moving at the speed national defense requires.”
Voyager said its motors typically use ammonium perchlorate as the oxidizer, combined with a liquid rubber binder and additives in a vacuum mixer to remove air bubbles before a curative solidifies the mixture in a cure oven. The company said it runs an in-house chemistry lab for raw material testing and process quality checks, and that one of its more complex propellants requires 84 separate quality tests on raw materials before production can begin. Voyager said samples are pulled during mixing and again before casting to test for properties including tensile strength, elongation and burn rate.
Voyager’s production model relies on a standardized library of propellant formulations that the company adapts to individual customer requirements, rather than developing new chemistry for each order. The company said small prototype motors have gone from contract to test fire in as few as three weeks, while more complex motors have taken roughly 180 days to complete and test fire.
“What differentiates Voyager is our library of proven propellant formulations that allows us to deliver without betting the program on unproven chemistry,” said Karl Kulling, general manager, Voyager Energetics. “We have the capability to innovate on the core chemistry when the mission demands it, but our default is to eliminate unnecessary risk and focus our innovation where it matters most: the manufacturing process.”
Voyager is building the Voyager American Defense Complex, a 150,000-square-foot (13,935-square-meter) facility at PuebloPlex in Pueblo, Colorado, the former U.S. Army Pueblo Chemical Depot. The company broke ground on the facility in January 2026 and has said the site will incorporate automation to handle steps in the production process that previously required workers to be near energetic materials. Voyager acquired the site’s existing operations, along with the broader solid rocket motor business, when it purchased Estes Energetics in November 2025. Matt Magaña has estimated the company’s total investment in the Pueblo site at approximately $100 million.
“For the rapid reindustrialization the Pentagon wants, solid rocket motor capabilities must be built and qualified in the U.S.,” Kulling said. “We have the certification, rigorous safety oversight and the strategic capacity to meet the moment’s urgency and deliver for national defense.”
Voyager has said the Pueblo facility is expected to become operational later in 2026. The company reported $84.3 million in Golden Dome missile defense contract awards during the second quarter of 2026, and has said its solid rocket propulsion and energetics work through Estes Energetics is intended to support the Space-Based Interceptor program’s kill vehicle propulsion requirements.

Iraq's parliament probes US-Saudi strikes on PMF HQ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:34:23 UTC
20:34:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq's parliament investigates US-Saudi strikes on PMF headquarters
Iraqi sources said the circumstances surrounding the US-Saudi strikes on the headquarters of Iraqi factions, which took place at the end of last month, remain unclear after statements circulated claiming that senior Iraqi leaders had advanced information of the strikes.
This prompted the Iraqi parliament's Security and Defence Committee to seek an investigation into the circumstances and host senior leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and prominent security officials to establish the facts and determine the details.
This strikes have set of growing repercussions, as well as doubts and questions raised in recent days about the security precautionary measures taken before the PMF headquarters were targeted and whether there had been any particular failure.
The committee, headed by MP Khalid al-Obeidi, issued an official letter inviting senior security and military officials, including PMF chief Falih al-Fayyadh and Chief of Staff Abdul Aziz al-Muhammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
Those invited also include the director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Abdul Amir al-Shammari; the army chief of staff, Abdul Amir Yarallah; and the senior Interior Ministry undersecretary, Hussein al-Awadi.
The letter stated that they would appear today at the committee's headquarters in the parliament building to determine why precautionary and security measures were not taken and why the headquarters was evacuated before the attack.
According to a member of the parliamentary committee, "The request to establish the facts and the attendance of the requested leaders came following accusations and statements that there had been advance information before the attack and that there had been a failure to perform the duty and evacuate the faction headquarters."
The member told The New Arab, on condition of anonymity, that "the committee is primarily focused on determining whether advance information about the strikes had reached the relevant agencies, which parties possessed it, and why urgent and decisive measures were not taken to address the situation before the airstrikes took place."
"The committee is carefully following the sequence of available intelligence information and the security measures that preceded the strikes to determine responsibilities and establish whether there were specific security gaps in the exchange of information and its intelligence verification and identify the parties or individuals responsible for this failure," the member added.
"Hosting the leaders and security officials will provide the committee with an opportunity to compare their statements with the information available to them," the source said, further stressing that "the hearings are part of an investigation that is not limited to determining the circumstances of the strike but also traces the information and establishes whether precautionary measures could have been taken in advance that might have prevented the casualties or reduced them."
The Iraqi government has repeatedly denied having prior knowledge of the strikes, but MPs and politicians have accused PMF leaders of possessing advance information about the targeting and failing to take sufficient precautions.
This has pushed the issue into a sensitive political arena that goes beyond the immediate security aspect.
Meanwhile, the PMF, which include the factions targeted in the strikes, rejected accusations against its chief, Falih al-Fayyadh, and claims that he had prior information about attacks on the headquarters and failed to inform the military units.
It described the accusations as "baseless claims that are not supported by any evidence or fact".
In a previous statement, the force said that "since the events in the region began months ago and until today, all its forces have been placed on alert, and two days before the strikes, all units were informed of the need to exercise the utmost caution and vigilance, which contributed to saving many lives and reducing the scale of the losses".
It said that "the fourth regiment of the 30th Brigade of the Popular Mobilisation did not take all the required preventive measures, resulting in the deaths of the largest number of its personnel during the attacks."
A sensitive issue
For his part, Iraqi political affairs specialist and academic Basim al-Azzawi said the issue was highly sensitive and that conflicting statements between accusations and denials involved political considerations.
He told TNA that "some parties may seek to use the issue of the strikes to achieve political gains, particularly given the sensitivity of the issue and its implications."
"The importance of the investigation lies in its ability to distinguish between security information and political responsibility and determine whether the failure, if established, resulted from weaknesses in the warning and information-sharing system, individual negligence by certain figures, or a broader failure in the management of the security issue," he added.
Iraqi official: PMF are part of armed forces
On Saturday, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said that "the PMF are part of the armed forces and that the decision to restrict weapons to the state targets entities operating outside the framework of the security institutions."
Maan made the remarks to the official Iraqi News Agency, INA.
"The PMF are part of the Iraqi armed forces, and their personnel are subject to the applicable military laws," he said.
He explained that "the entities covered by the restriction of weapons are those operating outside the framework of the state's security institutions".
"The PMF are part of the Iraqi armed forces, and under Law No. 40 of 2016, all its personnel are subject to the applicable military laws," Maan added.
He said that "the decision to restrict weapons to the state is intended to affirm that there is no parallel leadership or other leadership using weapons outside the framework of the state".
Sources inside the PMF in Iraq said on Wednesday, 12 August, that major changes are expected within the force, including the replacement of its current chief, Falih al-Fayyadh, who has been at this post since being formally appointed in 2020.
The changes also include the replacement of PMF Chief of Staff Abdul Aziz al-Muhammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
He emerged publicly and assumed his post after his predecessor, Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was assassinated by a US airstrike in January 2020.
The sources added to TNA that the changes are the first steps towards further integrating the PMF into Iraq's regular security and military system amid US pressure to restrict the weapons of Iran-aligned factions that are incorporated into and funded by the PMF itself.

Most political parties reject Swiss neutrality initiative
All major Swiss political parties except the right-wing Swiss People's Party oppose the neutrality initiative ahead of the September 27 vote, arguing that it would weaken Switzerland's security and foreign policy flexibility.
The popular initiative “Safeguarding Swiss Neutrality”, tabled by Pro Suisse and members of the People’s Party, seeks to define Swiss neutrality as “perpetual and armed”. It also demands that Switzerland not join any military or defence alliances, not participate in foreign wars and not impose economic or diplomatic sanctions against a belligerent state, subject to its obligations towards the United Nations.
For the opponents, the neutrality initiative “jeopardises our security, breaks with our values and severely restricts our capacity for external action”.
Switzerland must preserve its time-tested neutrality and not unnecessarily compromise its capacity for action in foreign and security policy, the committee said in a press release on Monday. It refuses to confine Switzerland to a rigid conception of neutrality.
More
Poll suggests little appetite for Swiss neutrality initiative
Bern must continue to cooperate with its international partners at a time when Europe is facing an increasingly unstable security situation. “When the emergency arises, it will, unfortunately, be far too late,” it said.
Furthermore, a form of neutrality that does not permit any sanctions, even in the face of the most flagrant violations of international law, runs counter to Swiss values, the opponents argue. This is all the more so given that the UN Security Council is increasingly paralysed by the veto rights of certain members, they add.

Billionaire Geely Auto head Li Shufu steps down as profit slips

How to avoid tick bites and diseases they spread this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:31:19 UTC
20:31:19 KST

Summer means long days outdoors — but across much of Europe, it also means peak tick season. The good news is that a few simple habits can substantially reduce the risk of being bitten.
Ticks are active across much of Europe from spring through autumn, and are commonly found in forests, grasslands, parks, gardens and other areas with vegetation. They can transmit diseases including Lyme borreliosis and tick-borne encephalitis (TBE).
The risk is not a reason to stay indoors. But a few minutes spent choosing protective clothing, applying repellent and checking for ticks afterwards can make outdoor time considerably safer.
The first rule is simple: make it harder for ticks to reach your skin
When walking through areas where ticks may be present, wear long trousers and long sleeves and tuck trousers into socks or boots. Light-coloured clothing can make ticks easier to spot. Where appropriate, use an approved insect repellent on exposed skin and clothing, following the product instructions.
It is also worth thinking about where you walk
Ticks tend to wait on vegetation for a host, so sticking to clear paths rather than brushing through long grass, dense undergrowth and bushes can reduce exposure. This is particularly relevant when hiking, camping, gardening or spending time in parks and woodland.
After spending time outdoors, check your entire body
Pay particular attention to skin folds, the groin, armpits, waist and the backs of the knees. Children’s heads and necks should also be checked carefully. Pets should be inspected too.
You got bitten? Don't panic
If you find a tick attached to your skin, remove it as soon as possible. As Lyme disease is unlikely to be transmitted within the first few hours after the bite, removing ticks attached to the skin as soon as possible reduces the risk. Using fine-tipped tweezers, grasp the tick as close to the skin as possible and pull it straight upwards, gently and without twisting or jerking. Then wash the bite and your hands with soap and water and apply an antiseptic.
When it comes to diseases...
Lyme disease is caused by bacteria and can generally be treated successfully with antibiotics. There is currently no licensed vaccine against Lyme disease, making bite prevention and early tick removal especially important.
TBE is different. It is caused by a virus and can affect the central nervous system, sometimes causing meningitis or encephalitis. There is no specific treatment for TBE, but vaccination is one of the most effective means of preventing TBE.

Tupac Shakur murder trial begins for alleged mastermind of 1996 drive-by shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:30:56 UTC
20:30:56 KST

A former street gang leader accused of masterminding the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas faces opening statements on Monday in a murder trial tied to a long-unsolved crime that became a seminal moment in rap history.
Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, is charged in Clark County, Nevada, with a single count of murder using a deadly weapon. He has pleaded not guilty. Davis is accused of leading a group of men to kill Shakur, 25, one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, in a 1996 drive-by shooting near the Las Vegas Strip.
The killing heightened the image of violence permeating hip-hop culture and its lyrics during "gangsta" rap's golden age, stoking the East Coast-West Coast rap feud of that era.
Police said after Davis' 2023 arrest that he was a longtime suspect in the killing but that investigators lacked sufficient admissible evidence to charge him until he began implicating himself in a series of public statements.
The trial before Judge Carli Kierny is expected to run for up to six weeks in a downtown Las Vegas courthouse. It may feature testimony from Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight, a former rap mogul who was with Shakur the night he was slain and is now serving a 28-year prison sentence on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction. A jury was selected last week.
The 'shot caller'
Authorities have described Davis as the "shot caller" of a hurried plot to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of his entourage inside the MGM Grand casino in Las Vegas the night of September 7, 1996.
The violence at the casino allegedly stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs -the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, which police say was associated with Knight and Death Row Records. They were in Las Vegas to see a world heavyweight title boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon.
Davis allegedly obtained the murder weapon and handed it off to two other men in the rear seat of a white Cadillac as they rode around looking for Knight and Shakur's car following the brawl.
Shots were fired when Davis and the others caught up with Knight and Shakur's vehicle. Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital six days later. Knight, who had been driving, suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head.
Cold case heats up
The murder investigation grew cold for years, but police said statements Davis made in 2018 to various media outlets about his involvement in the shooting reinvigorated the case.
Davis said in interviews and in his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend," that he was riding in the front passenger seat of the Cadillac and had handed the gun to one of the two men sitting behind him, according to police.
But neither Davis' account nor authorities have said who fired the gun at Shakur. The three other men in the Cadillac with Davis have all since died.
Under Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder if he took part in the crime without pulling the trigger.
In his book, Davis wrote that he was long considered a suspect in the murders of Shakur and a rival rapper, Christopher Wallace, who performed as The Notorious B.I.G. under the New York-based Bad Boy Entertainment label and was shot dead in Los Angeles in March 1997.
Although the Wallace killing remains unsolved, investigators have long speculated that he was gunned down in retaliation for Shakur's killing months earlier.

The Likud primary: Trolling as a way to gain support – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
11:30:49 UTC
20:30:49 KST

Israel’s governing-party primary has turned into a competition for grotesquerie. Israel Katz, the defense minister charged with protecting a country facing existential threats, opens with explosions: “Boom, boom, boom,” goes his AI-generated campaign song.
Yoav Kisch, a respected former IDF pilot and now an education minister apparently converted to trolling, joins the AI-song craze. Idit Silman – minister of something, presumably – floods social media with her customary graciousness.
Before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu blocked her from running, Hadar Muchtar, who has spent years trying to turn TikTok virality into a Knesset seat, made her pitch plainly: Young Israelis live on TikTok and Instagram, and she could deliver their votes to Netanyahu.
The bad taste has a function. Likud candidates are fighting for recognition in a crowded primary. A serious argument about education or defense cannot travel through WhatsApp groups the way a cringe clip, generated in seconds at almost no cost, will.
A viral clip keeps a minister in the public conversation without forcing him to explain what the government has actually delivered.
What the spectacle hides
The deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust occurred on this government’s watch. Israel has since inflicted severe damage on Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran and demonstrated extraordinary military capabilities. Yet after almost three years of war, the “total victory” repeatedly promised by Netanyahu is difficult to identify on any front.
Hamas’s disarmament remains remote. Hezbollah has been badly weakened, but the northern threat remains. Iran’s nuclear program was set back an estimated three to five years, yet enriched uranium remains in the country, the ballistic threat survives, and the regime that built both is still in power and openly committed to Israel’s destruction.
In June, only 15% of respondents in an INSS survey thought Israel had won the latest war against Iran.
Meanwhile, 968 Israeli soldiers have been killed since October 7. The war’s human and psychological costs are only beginning to surface.
In July, the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department reported 26,200 wounded from the current war in its care; 65% were seeking treatment for psychological distress or PTSD. It expects to be treating around 50,000 people with psychological injuries by 2028. Reservists make up 62% of the current-war wounded in the system.
The domestic record offers even less cinematic material.
Police figures recorded 309 murders in 2025. The haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft question has festered through years of war while the same reservists are repeatedly called back to duty. Political and social polarization has returned at an even higher level than before October 7: A May 2026 study measured it at 8.3 out of 10, above the level recorded during the 2023 judicial-overhaul crisis.
On the cost of living: Israel entered this government’s term already among the OECD’s most expensive countries. Food prices were 37% above the OECD average and 51% above the European Union in purchasing-power terms.
Since then, major household expenses have climbed another 15% to 30%. Netanyahu ran in 2022 on bringing prices down. His government’s committee on the cost of living met once.
Then there is the brain drain. A study published this month estimates that 268,509 Israelis left the country for at least three consecutive months between 2023 and 2025 – close to 90,000 a year, compared with roughly 60,000 annually in the previous decade.
Researchers found particularly worrying increases among doctors, engineers, PhDs, academics, and high earners. In 2024 alone, 530 doctors left Israel, roughly twice the previous annual norm.
For a small country whose economy, health system, military edge, and tax base depend heavily on skilled human capital, this is a strategic warning, and potentially a quasi-existential threat to its long-term viability as a modern society and economy.
There are some positive signs in the current chaos, but an impressively solid and resilient economy and exceptional IDF tactical achievements do not automatically add up to a safer, more cohesive, or better-governed country. In that context, “boom, boom, boom” starts to look like strategy rather than accident.
Netanyahu’s troll problem
Netanyahu cannot cast himself as the adult rescuing Likud from this degeneracy. He helped build the incentives that reward it. Long before generative AI, he understood the value of bypassing traditional mediation, personalizing politics, and speaking directly to the base.
The Likud trolls did not fall from the sky. They developed in an ecosystem where provocation became political capital. Tally Gotliv may be its purest product. Her politics runs on permanent confrontation, accusation, yelling, and spectacular language, and internal Likud polling has repeatedly placed her near the top.
TheMarker reported explicitly that Netanyahu feared the trollization of Likud’s top 10 and what that culture may look like on a national ballot. That helps explain the unusually large number of reserved slots he has accumulated to shape the upper part of the ticket.
Recent reporting linked the maneuver to his concern about Gotliv reaching the top 10 and his desire for a more mamlakhti slate capable of recovering moderate right-wing voters.
Even mamlakhtiyut changes meaning here. Traditionally, it referred to an ethic of state responsibility: restraint, institutional seriousness, an understanding that office imposes obligations on its holder.
In this primary, it functions more like casting: more respectable faces positioned high enough on the list to reassure voters about what the party’s internal market has produced underneath.
The Likud primary offers a compact portrait of Israeli politics in 2026. A government with a weak domestic record and an unresolved strategic one campaigns through synthetic images of strength.
The AI clips are ridiculous, but they are not incidental.
They belong to a governing culture particularly skilled at projecting power and far less convincing when asked what, concretely, it has delivered to Israelis.
The writer is a senior analyst in radical ideologies, cognitive security, and narrative warfare, a former Jerusalem Post journalist, and is completing a PhD in Digital Humanities at the Sorbonne.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the IDF’s planned transfer of West Bank civilian enforcement to Israel Police a “significant step toward Israeli sovereignty” on Monday.
Earlier, Defense Minister Israel Katz announced that the military will present a plan for the transfer within the next two weeks, after initially announcing intention for the transfer of authority on Friday. “We will not allow violence or unauthorized parties to take the law into their own hands,” Katz said.
In his response, Ben-Gvir hailed Katz's decision, noting it to be a "significant step toward [implementing] Israeli sovereignty in the West Bank.

Katz aiming to redefine IDF role in West Bank
On Friday, Katz had announced that he had instructed the IDF to prepare a plan to transfer all civilian enforcement authority for Israeli communities and residents in the West Bank to the Israel Police, as part of a broader effort to redefine the military's role in the territory.
The move came amid criticism levied at the military of its failure to control settler extremists, who in recent days have targeted Palestinian homes in the village of Kusra, dismantling fences, blocking roads, and besieging the area.

"The IDF's role is to fight Palestinian terrorism and focus on defending the borders and the communities against threats," Katz said in a statement. "All responsibility for enforcing civilian matters and maintaining law and order will be transferred to the police," he added.
The IDF has traditionally handled law and order in the West Bank because the territory is under military administration, while the Israel Police is responsible for civilian law enforcement inside Israel.

Africa is already the frontier – Botswana president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Africa is already the frontier – Botswana president
Botswana President Duma Boko has challenged the characterization of Africa as the world’s next major economic frontier, arguing that the continent has already reached that position and should deal with foreign partners accordingly.
African nations should approach investors from a position of strength rather than as supplicants, Boko told RT in an exclusive interview. He said governments must set their own conditions for access to resources, including local processing, technology deployment and skills transfers.
“Africa is actually the ‘now’ frontier,” Boko said.
The president said Botswana is also seeking deeper ties with Russia and is planning to open an embassy in Moscow. He noted that Russia is the only permanent member of the UN Security Council in which Botswana does not have a mission, describing the absence as an “anomaly” that needed to be corrected.
Botswana has never maintained a resident embassy in Moscow, despite diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union dating back to 1970. Russia can provide the expertise and technology needed to survey Botswana’s largely unexplored mineral resources, he added.
“We need these collaborations to explore the rest of the country, about 70% which remains largely unexplored,” the leader said.
Boko sees cooperation with Russia as important for Botswana’s diamond industry. He said the two countries need to work together to protect the market from oversupply.
He also argued that African economies have historically been geared toward extraction and the export of unprocessed resources, with insufficient emphasis on developing local industrial capabilities and skills.
“We now must focus on not being big on extraction, but take it all the way to actually producing finished goods, which the world needs,” he said.
Boko also backed the African Union’s push for reparative justice, saying developed economies benefited historically from African resources and should acknowledge the consequences of colonial exploitation.
