Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan represented a different kind of transformation, stressing that it presents "a real opportunity for us to deliver an important message to the world."
Speaking in an interview with Al Jazeera Arabic television, recorded on August 14, the day the governing Justice and Development (AK) Party celebrated its 25th anniversary, Erdogan said: "Coming together on such a day is truly a special joy for us."
"With our 25th anniversary celebrations, we will, God willing, continue our journey towards many more quarter-centuries," he said.
About the Mecca defence agreement recently signed by Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Erdogan said: "First of all, the Mecca agreement represented a different kind of transformation."
"The signing of this trilateral agreement in Mecca between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan became an opportunity for us to deliver an important message to the world," he said. "The fact that this agreement was concluded in Mecca and that we achieved it as three countries gave us additional strength and conveyed a separate message to the world."
"I believe that Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia all concluded this agreement with great satisfaction. May it be beneficial," he said.
Stressing that the pact was signed during a difficult period between the US and Iran, Erdogan said it conveyed an important message for world peace. "I call it an important message for world peace because Türkiye is a country that stands for peace, and the choice of Mecca has been an important step for peace," he said.
"During the process between Iran and the US, we consistently emphasised that we support peace," Erdogan said. "As countries pursuing such a process in favour of peace, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia have taken their place as advocates of peace."
"As defenders of peace, we will continue on this path as countries pursuing peace in the coming period," he stressed.
Collective defence provision
Asked whether the Mecca agreement resembles NATO's Article 5 collective defence provision, Erdogan said: "Whatever NATO's Article 5 includes, similarly, this common defence understanding means that if any problem arises, these three countries will have the opportunity to take the necessary steps together."
"Whether it concerns Türkiye, Saudi Arabia or Pakistan, if any one of these three countries comes under attack, because this is a common defence pact, the three countries will have the opportunity to defend one another against any such attack," he emphasised.
"Beyond these three countries, others may join us at any time," he said. "It is not limited to Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan."
"Additional countries may also become part of it. When we signed the agreement, we announced that if other countries wished to join in the future, our door would remain open. We have kept that door open."
"If Egypt wishes, these three countries can reach an agreement and open the door to Egypt as well," the Turkish president added.
US war on Iran
Regarding the war involving the US, Israel and Iran, Erdogan said his wish was for peace to be achieved at the earliest.
Pointing out that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil consumption flowed before the war, was causing difficulties, Erdogan said: "We need to reopen this traffic as soon as possible and ensure that the world's oil traffic flows again without interruption."
"We support this, and Iran supports it as well,” he said. "Our hope is that if maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is reopened free of charge, it will be far more appropriate."
"Free passage would be highly beneficial in reopening traffic there."
Asked about Türkiye's position on US-Israeli attacks on Iran and Tehran's retaliatory attacks on Gulf countries, Erdogan said: "We are definitely not in favour of war."
"We are in favour of peace. But Israel is the main actor behind this war," he said, adding: “Israel has consistently encouraged war and chosen war. Because of this stance, many other countries have paid a heavy price. Israel bears the main responsibility."
Visit to Damascus
Regarding Qatar's and Pakistan's mediation efforts between the US and Iran, the Turkish president said both countries had undertaken important responsibilities and expressed confidence that they would continue to do so.
"We will all join hands and, first and foremost, preserve our unity and solidarity as Muslims," he said.
Speaking about relations with Syria's new administration led by President Ahmed al Sharaa and Israel's attacks on Syria, Erdogan said: "Our state institutions have very good relations with Syria, and we are maintaining this unity and solidarity."
"Syria is our sibling. We will never leave Syria alone. During this process, Syria will see the attention and support of its siblings. They should have no concerns," he stressed.
About Türkiye's support for Syria's stability, Erdogan said: "Whatever Türkiye must do for Syria's stability, we are doing it to the fullest extent and will continue to do so."
Regarding Ankara's role in the process leading to the fall of Bashar al Assad's regime, Erdogan said: "Thank God, President Sharaa and his colleagues know very well what we have done."
"We fulfilled every responsibility that fell upon us, and we will continue to do so in the coming period. I will, God willing, visit Damascus as soon as possible."
Israeli attacks on Lebanon
He also spoke about Israeli attacks on Lebanon, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's visit to Türkiye and bilateral relations.
"These attacks against Lebanon deeply sadden us," he said. “We held talks with the president here. In the coming period, we will continue to provide whatever support we can to Lebanon."
The president stressed the importance of US support for the peace process in Lebanon, saying: "By achieving this, we must save Lebanon from this ring of fire."
On Israel's attacks on Lebanon, Erdogan said: "At present, Israel is the aggressor.”
"Lebanon remains under continuous Israeli attacks," he said, adding: "We must free Lebanon from these attacks as soon as possible."
"We discussed this issue with the US and will continue to do so. I also discussed it with Mr. (Donald) Trump during his visit to Türkiye, and we will continue our talks with him in the coming period," he said.
'We cannot leave Gaza on its own'
On Israel's continuing attacks on Gaza, despite a ceasefire in October 2025, Erdogan said: "We cannot leave Gaza on its own. Whatever responsibility falls upon us regarding Gaza, we have fulfilled it until today and will continue to do so."
Commenting on Hamas's acceptance of the ceasefire provisions, including moving to the second phase, giving up governance in Gaza and agreeing to give up its weapons, Erdogan said: "Hamas has demonstrated all the sincere solidarity it could, but there has been no such positive approach from Israel.”
"Israel continues its aggressive policies by attacking Lebanon and Gaza," he criticised.
Referring to his discussions with the US president regarding Israel, Erdogan said: "I see that Trump is disturbed by these developments. We are also making every necessary warning, and we will continue to do so."
Asked about hostile rhetoric towards Türkiye by Israeli politicians and media outlets, Erdogan said: "If anyone chooses to attack Türkiye for war rather than peace, Türkiye will neither fear nor avoid such a war."
"I say this very clearly. We do not wish to experience such a situation."
Relations with Sudan
Touching on relations with Sudan, where a civil war continues since 2023, Erdogan said: "I do not view developments in Sudan positively, but we continue to provide every possible support to Sudan."
"My relations" with Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the chairman of Sudan’s Sovereignty Council are "very good," he said, adding that "Sudan truly has a moderate and ideal administration."
Burhan "was recently our guest, and we held talks together. I genuinely see Sudan's leader as a leader worthy of Sudan at this stage," Erdogan said.
On developments in Libya, Erdogan said: "Our relations with Libya continue firmly."
"We will not leave Libya alone in the steps it is taking," he said. "In particular, as Turkish Petroleum, we have taken and continue to take steps to jointly develop Libya's oil reserves."
F-35 programme
On relations with the US, Erdogan said: "At present, we expect Mr. Trump to fulfill the promise he made regarding the F-35 fighter jets."
"He made a commitment to us concerning the F-35s, and fulfilling this promise is important for Türkiye. We expect this commitment to be honoured," he said.
Asked about the most important issues between Türkiye and the US, Erdogan said: "There are issues related to the defence industry. Besides, there are the steps we have taken and will take regarding trade volume," he said.
Emphasising that Israel was not part of Türkiye-US relations, Erdogan said: "We have never placed Israel on the table in our discussions."
"Our counterpart is the US,” he said. "We take and will continue to take our steps by discussing these issues with the US."
Relations with Russia, EU, Arab world
On ties with Moscow, Erdogan said: "Our relations with Russia are very good. We maintain them through continuous telephone diplomacy."
"My ministers regularly speak with their Russian counterparts, and they also contact my ministers. In this way, we continue our consultations," he said.
Responding to questions about Türkiye's relations with the EU, Erdogan said: "Europe has not admitted Türkiye for 53 years, and it does not appear willing to do so in the future either."
"But we have not closed our door," he said. "We still want to join the EU."
Erdogan said EU membership was not Türkiye’s priority, arguing the bloc would lose if it rejected Ankara. He stressed Türkiye’s military strength and unity while calling for solidarity with the Arab world.

41 percent of people who saw heat alerts took no action, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:03:21 UTC
19:03:21 KST

Heatwaves are becoming more frequent and severe - but a new study finds that 41% of people who saw heat-health alerts in England took no protective action. Why aren't warnings translating into action?
This summer's heat has been extreme. Successive heatwaves have dried out landscapes, melted glaciers, shrunk lakes and rivers, while wildfires have scorched vast areas, leaving landscapes dramatically transformed.
But the effects of extreme heat go far beyond what we can see in the landscape. And one of the most serious consequences of extreme heat is harder to see: the impact on our health.
Despite repeated warnings from health officials, many people in England still do not see extreme heat as a serious health risk.
A new investigation by experts at the United Nations University has found a significant gap between heat-health warnings and people's behaviour. The study looked at how people respond to heat-health alerts (HHAs) and why warnings do not always lead to protective action.
The researchers surveyed 1,097 adults in England and interviewed 29 people involved in communicating heat risks.
What people know does not always translate into action
The results reveal a clear gap between what people know about heat and what they actually do about it.
Around seven in 10 people surveyed had encountered a Heat Health Alert. But among those who had seen an alert, 41 percent reported taking no action to protect themselves.
The most common reason was simple: they did not believe they were personally at risk.
Only 18.1 percent of people said they perceived a high risk from extreme heat. Around 30 percent also said they had limited or no knowledge of the actions that could protect them.
The reasons for not acting varied. Nineteen percent cited a low perception of their personal risk. Nine percent did not recognise the alert, while 7 percent were unsure what action to take and 5 percent found the alert difficult to understand.
So why are people not responding to warnings?
The researchers say that simply sending out an alert is not enough. People need to understand that extreme heat can pose a risk to their health, recognise when a warning applies to them and know what they can do to protect themselves.
How those warnings are delivered may also be part of the problem.
Ninety percent of the heat-risk communicators interviewed said they used digital channels. These allow information to spread quickly, but they do not necessarily reach everyone equally. Social media was identified as the least trusted source of heat information, particularly among older adults.
Around 30 percent of people reported not encountering heat-health alerts or heat-protection information at all. That creates a worrying mismatch: the channels used to communicate heat risks do not always reach the people who are most vulnerable to them.
How to reach people beyond the digital world
The researchers also recommend using trusted local organisations - including community groups, libraries, social care providers, voluntary organisations and faith groups - to reach people who may be missed by digital warnings.
The researchers say authorities also need to get better at measuring whether their communication actually works. Instead of simply counting website visits, social media engagement or media coverage, they should assess whether people understand the warnings and whether those warnings lead to protective action.
Make heat warnings clearer and more actionable
The interviews with heat-risk communicators point to another problem. Heat communication in England is largely focused on coordination between institutions and emergency preparedness, rather than on helping people change their behaviour.
The researchers say informing people is currently the dominant objective. But informing alone may not be enough to motivate people to take protective action.
And communication is only part of the problem.
The study also points to more fundamental factors that determine who is vulnerable to extreme heat. These include housing conditions, socioeconomic disadvantage, existing health problems, environmental exposure and access to resources.
A warning cannot address those factors.
Beyond warnings: making homes and communities more resilient
As heatwaves become more frequent and severe, the researchers argue that England needs to move beyond a predominantly warning-based approach.
That means improving how heat risks are communicated, but also making longer-term changes to reduce people's exposure and vulnerability.
Housing is a key part of that. The researchers call for heat resilience to be integrated into housing standards, planning policies and retrofit programmes, including stronger implementation and enforcement of measures designed to reduce overheating in buildings.
The challenge, the researchers say, is therefore not just to warn people that the next heatwave is coming - but to make sure fewer people are vulnerable when it arrives.

Israel sees 53% drop of returnees as departures on rise: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:02:58 UTC
19:02:58 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Lina Altawell
17 August 2026•Update: 17 August 2026
A recent official Knesset report showed a sharp decline in the number of Israelis returning to Israel in recent years, alongside a rise in the number of those leaving the country, Yedioth Ahronoth reported Monday.
“The wave of hostility towards Israel in the world and the sense of belonging could have led to an increase in the number of Israelis returning, despite the war,” the newspaper said citing a report by the Knesset Research and Information Center
The report comes amid widespread public and official anger toward Israel around the world over its US-backed genocidal war on Gaza since Oct. 8, 2023.
The genocide has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, most of them women and children, while destroying 90% of Gaza’s infrastructure. The UN has estimated reconstruction costs at around $70 billion.
“In the years 2022-2024, there was a drastic 53% decrease in the number of returning residents,” the Knesset report highlighted, according to the newspaper.
The report did not address the proportion of Israelis returning in 2025.
The newspaper said the decline coincides with recently published data by Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics and academic researchers showing a sharp increase in the number of Israelis leaving the country.
“The study also addressed a series of bureaucratic, economic, and social challenges that make it difficult for Israelis to make a decision to return,” the newspaper said.
These include long waiting periods to obtain state health insurance, fewer benefits compared with new immigrants, employment challenges and difficulties integrating children into the education system.
Yedioth Ahronoth said the average annual number of returning Israelis stood at around 9,300 between 2008 and 2012, before falling to around 7,400 between 2013 and 2020.
“There has been a steep decrease in the number of returnees from about 8,000 in 2020 to about 3,800 in 2024 - the lowest number in recent years,” it said.
According to the newspaper, the report said the steepest decline occurred in 2023, without providing further details.
The drop in return migration also contributed to Israel’s migration balance deficit between 2022 and 2024, which measures the difference between those entering and leaving the country.
According to Central Bureau of Statistics data cited in the report, Israel recorded a migration deficit of around 140,000 people over those three years.
The newspaper said North America has long accounted for the largest share of returning Israelis, but the number returning from there has also fallen sharply.
Around half of all returnees between 2005 and 2024 came from North America, while another 13% returned from Britain, Germany and France, and 6% from Russia and Ukraine.
The number of returnees from the US dropped significantly, from around 3,700 in 2020 to only 1,500 in 2024.
“The proportion of residents returning from Russia and Ukraine increased significantly in 2022 to 9% from Ukraine and 8% from Russia of all returnees, apparently due to the Russia-Ukraine war,” the newspaper said.

Stubborn vulture plucked from plane’s wing before Greece flight

Other local sites showed a picture of the vulture landing on the plane’s tail wing.

Birds are routinely sucked into aircraft engines, occasionally causing serious accidents.

Four suspected bird strikes to the plane’s engine were reported by flight crews in the 12 months preceding the accident, but no damage was found in subsequent maintenance, the report said. AFP

Far-right FVD-linked school opens in Almere with state funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:02:19 UTC
19:02:19 KST

Far-right FVD-linked school opens in Almere with state funding
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A primary school linked to the far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD) has opened with state funding in Almere, teaching pupils that “the old Europe was better than the new,” and doing away with the “dogma of equality”.
The “Renaissance School” started with one class of 18 four and five-year-olds. Its founders say the curriculum follows the view of humanity found in classical antiquity, the middle ages and the early modern period.
The school’s site says it approaches scientific views such as climate change as “falsifiable theories” and that boys and girls may be taught differently in recognition of biological differences, NRC reported.
School head Douwe Filz told De Telegraaf that classes are mixed and there are no separate subjects for boys or girls, although material may be presented in different ways.
Pupils are taught Latin and English alongside Dutch, and the school works with printed books, has no wifi and makes limited use of computers.
FVD has presented its Renaissance schools as an answer to what it calls left-wing indoctrination in the classroom, a theme it has pursued since setting up a reporting hotline for pupils in 2019. Ralf Dekker, who led the project for the party, told NOS in 2022 there would be “no woke thinking in the teaching material”.
The school is run by Stichting Tocqueville, formally separate from FVD, although several of its board members and staff are active in the party. Party chairman Thierry Baudet has described it as part of an FVD pillar alongside the party itself.
Questions in parliament
 VVD MP Arend Kisteman and D66 MP Ilana Rooderkerk have written parliamentary questions about the school, which will be answered when parliament reconvenes after August 31.
“It is too easy to set up a small school in the Netherlands,” Kisteman told De Telegraaf. “That worsens the teacher shortage and the taxpayer picks up the bill.”
Rooderkerk told the paper she wanted inspectors to step in before four-year-olds were indoctrinated with FVD’s ideas. Judith Tielen, the VVD junior education minister, is drawing up options for tightening the rules and said inspectors would carry out a full quality inspection within the school’s first year.
The Dutch constitution has allowed publicly funded faith and worldview schools since 1917. Most of those founded since a 2020 law relaxed the rules are faith schools, the biggest share of them are Islamic.
Market research tactics
 Schools seeking state funding normally have to collect 100 signed declarations from parents, which FVD failed to do.
Instead, the school’s backers used market research to show that the population of the area will increase, boosting the need for a new school.
An earlier attempt to open the Renaissance School in Almere, which was fully funded by parents and private sources, failed and closed in 2024.

Moscow court sentences Lithuanian man for removing plaques on Soviet burial site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:02:00 UTC
19:02:00 KST

A Moscow court has sentenced Lithuanian citizen Romas Liutkus to seven years in prison in absentia for allegedly damaging the graves of Soviet soldiers in Lithuania, Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office said.
The court also imposed a five-year ban on activities related to the administration of websites and telecommunications networks, according to a statement from the prosecutor’s office.
Liutkus rejected the charges, saying he removed three Lithuanian-language plaques from the site in September 2024 but did not damage any graves. He said his actions were aimed at removing what he considered propaganda and historically inaccurate inscriptions, rather than targeting the deceased soldiers.
Russian prosecutors alleged that Liutkus, motivated by political and ideological hatred of Russia and acting with unidentified accomplices, damaged a burial site for 119 Soviet soldiers killed in 1944 in Krekenava, in central Lithuania’s Panevėžys district.
The Moscow court found Liutkus guilty of damaging soldiers’ graves outside Russia and insulting the memory of Soviet soldiers.
Liutkus said he handed the undamaged plaques over to the local elder of Krekenava. The incident was investigated by Lithuanian police and the Department of Cultural Heritage, but neither institution found any violations of Lithuanian law, he said.
In 2024, Lithuania’s Desovietisation Commission concluded that the monument at the site violated a ban on promoting totalitarian and authoritarian regimes. The monument consisted of an obelisk topped with a star and inscriptions in Lithuanian and Russian reading “Eternal Memory to the Fallen Soviet Soldiers”, along with granite plaques.
The Soviet soldiers are buried in a communal cemetery in Krekenava.
Liutkus said he learned about the Moscow court’s verdict through public reports and had not received any summonses to court hearings or interrogations.
He said he was aware that he could not travel to certain countries where a Russian request for his detention could be enforced.
The case comes amid heightened tensions between Lithuania and Russia following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine and Lithuania’s efforts to remove symbols associated with the Soviet Union.

WATCH hundreds of migrants demand asylum in Spanish enclave

19:01:53 KST

WATCH hundreds of migrants demand asylum in Spanish enclave
Hundreds of Moroccan migrants have protested in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, demanding asylum as thousands remain stranded in the area following mass border crossings last month.
The crisis erupted on July 30-31, when an estimated 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta from neighboring Morocco – equivalent to roughly 70% of the enclave’s population of around 84,000. While most returned shortly afterward, an estimated 7,000 to 9,000 remain, straining reception centers, hospitals, and law enforcement.
The influx has triggered a bitter dispute over the migrants’ fate. Ceuta Mayor-President Juan Jesus Vivas has called for asylum claims linked to the surge to be rejected and migrants returned to Morocco.
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska backed the hardline approach last week, saying irregular arrivals would not be allowed to remain in Ceuta, reach mainland Spain, or obtain legal status, except in rare cases of extreme vulnerability. Judicial associations have pushed back, insisting claims must be assessed individually and that illegal entry does not forfeit the right to seek asylum.
Amid the row, several hundred migrants staged a sit-in on a popular Ceuta beach on Sunday, urging the Spanish authorities not to return them to Morocco. Footage shows protesters waving Spanish flags and banners while chanting: “We need asylum!”
“We Moroccans are protesting without food or water, we will continue sitting here,” one protester told the Ruptly video agency. Separate footage shows security forces detaining several migrants on the beach, though it is unclear if they were part of the protest.
The initial surge came shortly after Spain’s Supreme Court ruled that migrants intercepted at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla, another Spanish enclave, could not be immediately deported. Spanish officials have accused trafficking networks of exploiting the ruling through viral social media posts falsely claiming the country’s borders were open.
Another wave of nearly 300 migrants attempted to enter Ceuta on Saturday but was stopped by Moroccan police, according to state broadcaster Medi 1 TV. Another 61 Moroccans accused of facilitating the attempt were arrested, the broadcaster said.
Brussels sticks to sidelines as migrant row deepens
Multiple EU members have pinned the blame for the Ceuta crisis squarely on Madrid and its permissive approach toward migration. Leaders of 22 EU nations accused Spain of undermining the bloc’s security in an August letter, with several calling for its exclusion from the Schengen borderless travel zone. Italy introduced temporary checks on travelers arriving from Spain on August 1, while France tightened border security.
Madrid hit back, branding the measures and criticism “selfish,” “polarizing,” and “unlawful.” It retaliated against Italy’s move by imposing reciprocal restrictions on travelers arriving from the country starting August 8.
Brussels, meanwhile, has largely sought to sit out the increasingly bitter dispute. The European Commission has refrained from penalizing Spain over the Ceuta crisis and praised Madrid for preventing irregular migrants from reaching mainland Europe, while dismissing calls for Schengen restrictions. However, it has also stopped short of offering Madrid substantial backing, so far limiting its response to sending a team of migration experts to Ceuta to assess what additional financial and operational support may be needed to secure the EU’s external border.
Migration has become an increasingly explosive issue in the EU, fueled partly by high-profile sexual abuse and assault cases involving migrants. Critics say Brussels’ asylum protections, burden-sharing schemes, and expanded legal migration pathways have created incentives for illegal migrants.
Commenting on the crisis, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also blamed EU migration policies, suggesting that “migrants are coming en masse to personally thank Ursula [von der Leyen] and other migration-friendly EU bureaucrats for their great migration incentives.” In a separate post, he warned that the “failure to admit migration mistakes is undermining what is left of Europe.”

Rhossi, a rare sea turtle, recovers after 5,000-mile trek from Wales to Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:00:52 UTC
19:00:52 KST

A Kemp’s ridley sea turtle native to the Gulf of Mexico is largely thriving after he was found nearly dead on a beach in Wales in late 2023, nursed back to health and then flown to Houston recently to continue recovering – though scans revealed signs that the creature has been grappling with lingering pneumonia, according to his caretakers.
Rhossi’s condition was detailed in a blogpost on Friday from the Houston zoo, whose veterinary team was tasked with caring for the creature – believed to be no older than age four – and giving him the best chance possible at an eventual, successful return to the wild.
A local dog discovered a 2lb (0.9kg), cold-stunned Rhossi, belonging to one of the world’s most endangered sea turtle species, on a beach in a Welsh village in December 2023. Rhossi was about 5,000 miles (8,000km) from the Gulf of Mexico region where Kemp’s ridley sea turtles are native – and from where they have been known to be swept away for vast distances, including across the Atlantic Ocean, by powerful marine currents.
Wales’s Anglesey Sea zoo subsequently took Rhossi in and spent the next two years nursing him to health again. His frame had more than tripled, and he had bulked up to 46lb (21kg) before he took a helicopter ride from Wales to London’s Heathrow airport – and then a transatlantic flight to Houston on 10 August.
The Houston zoo’s sea turtle staff by then had committed to taking over the administration of Rhossi’s recovery, the facility said in its blogpost on Friday. And after an initial evaluation, Rhossi’s caretakers placed him in a deep-water tank to let him become acclimated to his new surroundings.
Rhossi then had a more comprehensive medical examination performed by Dr Joe Flanagan, a senior veterinarian who briefly came out of retirement for the assessment, the Houston zoo said.
The resilient turtle had his organ function, eyes, mouth, shell and flippers checked. He also had X-rays and a CT scan to take a closer look at his lungs, according to the Houston zoo.
Rhossi largely acquitted himself as “healthy, active and vigorous” during the examination, the facility reported.
“He’s very strong,” Flanagan said in a Reuters video report. “He swims normally. He dives. He surfaces. He breathes fine.”
But, after having endured the north Atlantic’s perilously frigid waters before his rescue, “his scans revealed a concern for lingering pneumonia”, and his return to the Gulf of Mexico would evidently “take a little longer than expected”, the zoo wrote.
The zoo nonetheless added: “Rhossi’s medical team will continue to monitor him and provide additional treatment, as needed, to ensure the best possible chance of a successful return to the wild.”
Houston’s zoo said Rhossi’s story illustrated the “incredible dedication and careful coordination of … multiple agencies and non-profit organizations”. The facility specifically mentioned the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Anglesey Sea and Houston zoos, the Texas state aquarium and the Welsh helicopter pilot Darren Briggs.
Underlying those entities’ efforts is the fact that the population of nesting Kemp’s ridley females is estimated to be only between 7,000 and 9,000, according to the Sea Turtle Conservancy.
The US government furthermore has considered Kemp’s ridleys as endangered since 1970, at risk of extinction within the foreseeable future because of threats from humans such as egg collection and killing for products such as meat, information from the conservancy says.
Frankie Hobro, the Anglesey Sea zoo director and owner, expressed high hopes for Rhossi as he settled into the Houston phase of his recovery.
“It looks like in a couple of years, he’ll be fit for breeding out in the wild,” Hobro said in the Reuters video. “So that’s really exciting news for us.”

====================================================================================================

Trump’s tough-guy image has been undone by his own actions | Mohamad Bazzi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:00:52 UTC
19:00:52 KST

For decades, Donald Trump cultivated a public image based on strength and dominance. He was a brash New York real estate mogul; a reality TV star who deployed his signature phrase: “You’re fired!” to eliminate contestants from The Apprentice; and eventually US president and undisputed leader of the Republican party.
In recent months, Trump has taken his boastfulness to an extreme, reportedly telling confidants that he’s “the most powerful person to ever live” and comparing himself with some of history’s most feared leaders, including Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin and Mao.
But recent revelations have threatened to shatter Trump’s image as a strongman: the US president departed on a secret military flight out of Turkey after attending a Nato summit, while the White House told the public he was flying onboard Air Force One. The operation involved an elaborate ruse in which Trump boarded his jumbo jet in view of TV cameras, and then was hustled out by the Secret Service through an airport catering truck. Trump was taken to an alternate military aircraft, which flew him to Britain – all unbeknown to journalists and several White House staff members who stayed on Air Force One and thought they were on the same plane as the president.
The embarrassing necessity was a result of Trump’s unnecessary war against Iran. US officials used such levels of subterfuge because they were worried about an Iranian assassination attempt against Trump, according to reports in the Washington Post and New York Times. On 11 August, Trump confirmed that he had secretly switched planes in Turkey, and attributed the decision to his protective detail and military advisers. “I go by Secret Service and the military,” Trump told reporters who asked why US officials had used such an intricate ploy and kept the public in the dark about it until the story was leaked. “They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane. Equal safety. But they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say.”
Trump tried to evade criticism that the decision left several cabinet members and senior White House officials – including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary; Stephen Miller, Trump’s top domestic adviser; and Steven Cheung, the White House communications director – on Air Force One to serve as decoys, along with other Trump staffers and journalists. To deflect more questions, Trump claimed, without providing evidence, that the secret military plane he flew on was actually at “greater risk” than the Air Force One jet that the world saw him board after the Nato summit. “I think it was at greater risk because that would be the plane I think that they would be more likely to go for,” he said.
It’s easy to see why Trump and his administration did not want to publicly share details of the ruse after the danger had passed, as past presidents had done when they used subterfuge to visit war zones and other hazardous locations. The image of Trump hiding in an airport catering container to avoid a potential Iranian assassination attempt is a stark contrast to the tough guy brand he spent years cultivating. It’s also an antithesis to the image Trump projected after he survived an assassination attempt at a presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. In a series of photos captured by news photographers at the scene, Trump raised his fist in the air and mouthed the words: “Fight, fight, fight” to supporters as he was rushed off stage by Secret Service agents, bleeding from his ear. One image in particular, showing a bloodied Trump pumping his fist with a US flag in the background, became iconic – and his campaign quickly tried to monetize it by using the photo on the cover of a book and to sell $299 Trump-branded sneakers.
Beyond the dueling imagery, the fact that Trump took refuge in a catering truck has deeper political implications. It encapsulates Trump’s failure in his war on Iran: a president who constantly boasts about US military prowess and tries to project personal strength instead appears weak in front of the world as he hides from the consequences of his own actions. Nearly six months ago, Trump launched his reckless war against Iran as an act of imperial hubris – and a culmination of a series of lawless acts since he returned to office in 2025.
With little resistance from the Republican-controlled Congress or the US supreme court, Trump was able to gut government agencies, use federal law enforcement to target his political enemies, appoint his loyalists as top prosecutors, deploy national guard troops into US cities, and weaken decades-old anti-corruption laws designed to constrain presidential power after the Watergate scandal. He also steamrolled over Congress and its authority to declare war.
In late February, when the US and Israel launched a series of devastating airstrikes against Iran, Trump had expansive goals: to destroy Tehran’s military capabilities and nuclear program, and to topple Iran’s theocratic regime by decimating its leadership and instigating a popular uprising. In the war’s early days, the US and Israel assassinated more than 30 senior Iranian military and political officials, including the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. But the Iranian system proved resilient and it quickly replaced those officials, partly by appointing Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba, as the new supreme leader, to ensure continuity.
Iran also turned its proximity to the strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which more than a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed each day, into an effective economic weapon. Tehran closed the passageway at the start of the war, increasing energy prices and disrupting the global economy. Since then, Trump has struggled to reach a deal with Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz and prevent the war from spiraling into a regional conflict that could cause severe economic damage.
For months, Trump has tried to negotiate a face-saving agreement that would allow him to declare victory and shift US public attention away from the war before midterm elections in November that could see Republicans lose control of Congress. Iran’s leaders and Trump both say they don’t trust the other side to abide by any agreement – and a memorandum of understanding reached in mid-June, which included reopening the strait of Hormuz and lifting a US naval blockade against Iranian ships in the region, has collapsed. Since then, tit-for-tat attacks by Iran and the US have rekindled fears of another all-out war.
Not surprisingly, Iranian officials and state media are reveling in the extensive media attention over Trump secretly switching planes in Turkey – and especially the detail about him being ushered into an airport catering truck. A presenter on Iranian state TV called it a “scandal stemming from fear of Iran’s military power”, and described the incident as a source of “humiliation” for the US president.
It will take time for Trump to undo the damage this ruse has done to his self-proclaimed image as a strong and dominant world leader. More importantly, his disastrous decision to launch a war against Iran will shape his legacy long after he leaves office.
- 
  Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

VCUARTS QATAR: أغرب إدراك | AGHRAB IDRĀK: THRESHOLDS OF PERCEPTION
As an Official Collateral Event of the Venice Biennale, Virginia Commonwealth University School of the Arts in Qatar (VCUarts Qatar) debuts the collective exhibition أغرب إدراك | Aghrab Idrāk: Thresholds of Perception, running from June 01 to November 22, 2026, at the historic Palazzo Cavanis at the Zattere. Co-curated by Dr. Hesperia Iliadou and Chase Westfall, the presentation aggregates ten interdisciplinary research labs from the university‘s Institute for Creative Research (ICR). Spanning robotics, spatial typography, soundscapes, and nanotechnology, the exhibition functions not as a passive display of finished artifacts, but as a chorus of live, material, and sensory investigations that challenge Western-centric methodologies and terra-centric perspectives.
‘For VCUarts Qatar, being selected as an Official Collateral Event of the Venice Biennale is an opportunity to share work that has emerged from years of creative research in our community in Qatar,’ begins Amir Berbić, Dean, VCUarts Qatar, in an exclusive video interview with designboom. ‘At the heart of the exhibition is the belief that creative research does more than reflect culture — it actively participates in shaping how we understand it.’
exhibition أغرب إدراك | Aghrab Idrāk: Thresholds of Perception | all images courtesy of VCUarts Qatar
TWO DISTINCT WORLD VIEWS UNITED UNDER A SINGULAR CREATIVE PULSE
The exhibition reflects the global footprint of VCUarts, an institution uniquely operating across two very different cultural landscapes: Richmond, Virginia, and Doha, Qatar. These dual campuses act as vital incubators where faculty, students, and alumni collaborate across disciplines, bound by a shared ethos of relentless experimentation and critical reflection. Backed by a long-standing partnership with the Qatar Foundation, the Institute for Creative Research generates innovative design through an ethical, human mode of inquiry, cultivating ideas that address complex social, cultural, and environmental questions without simple answers.
‘Through VCUarts Qatar, creative research serves as a mode of inquiry and innovation,’ adds VCU President Michael Rao, PhD. ‘It offers ways of understanding complex social, cultural and environmental questions that are both rigorous and deeply human.’
as vital incubators the hubs develop collaborative design solutions for pressing social and environmental challenges
A DEEP DIVE INTO MULTI-SENSORY EXPERIMENTS AND MATERIAL HISTORIES
Stepping into the rooms of Palazzo Cavanis, visitors encounter independent yet interconnected landscapes of sound, craft, and technology arranged in an unfolding sequence of ecological and material narratives. In Mapping Migration Memories by the (IN)>Tangible Lab, familial oral histories and seasonal desert routes are rendered into a dense, textured soundscape that establishes the desert as a living environment rather than an abstraction. This fluid perspective continues in the GA:MA Lab’s Oceans & Lands: Drifting Senses and Knowledges, where historical objects like a colonial desk and a sailor’s trunk are layered with fabrics, spices, and audio to trace transcultural traumas and drifting across the Indian Ocean.
exploring the landscape as a living environment, Mapping Migration Memories translates oral histories and seasonal desert routes
Communication itself is structurally re-imagined in TypeAraby’s Bandhani Arabi: From Thread to Word, a project that collaborates with Muslim women artisans in Bhuj, India, to use the traditional tie-dye craft of Bandhani as a generative matrix for constructing Arabic typographic letterforms. Nearby, Sonic Jeel’s Sonic Fields uses a modular synthesizer to stretch and blend Doha’s public field recordings — from harbor dhow boats to World Cup echoes — into an unpredictable, shifting acoustic archive of a city in transition.
the exhibition layout sequences independent zones to highlight evolving ecological and material narratives
The physical boundaries between nature and machinery blur as visitors advance through the remaining spaces. Boost Lab’s Chrysalis introduces an animate, breathing mechanical sculpture that actively purifies contaminated air, its rhythmic respiration prompting a reflection on planetary fragility and cohabitation. In The Gulf Between Us by Water With Water, a five-year crowdsourced photography zine expands into a three-dimensional installation of suspended, layered large-format prints, building a collective, non-hierarchical portrait of life in the region. The social margins of the Gulf are further explored by the Anthro-tech Atelier in Whispers from United Geekdom, which utilizes intimate video portraits and a modular grid to celebrate the creative empowerment and identity definition within local gaming, cosplay, and role-playing subcultures.
a breathing kinetic sculpture designed to actively purify contaminated air through a rhythmic mechanical system
Technology increasingly acts as both an architectural and philosophical mirror toward the end of the exhibition. Addressing the Latin alphabet bias embedded within contemporary digital infrastructure, xLab’s Preceding Emptiness utilizes a structural grid of 60cm LED tubes — inspired by the historic geometry of square Kufic inscriptions — to build a large-scale digital ecology for Arabic script. This is paired with Mesh Lab’s A Monocular Monologue, where a 3D-printed, single-eyed robotic creature fixes its gaze on the viewer, endlessly whispering poetic ruminations that position modern artificial intelligence within the lineage of ancient myth and human ambition. Finally, AlBokeh Lab presents … and I Was Left Behind راحوا و خلوني, a visceral documentary film that uses the tactile, repetitive labor of textile repair to archive the deep emotional bonds that withstand the trauma of migration, separation, and political borders in the Gulf.
the repetitive act of textile repair explores emotional endurance, migration, and political borders across the gulf region
The Arabic phrase aghrab idrāk translates to ‘strange knowledge’ or ‘unusual perception,’ evoking historical philosophical dialogues between the ancient Greek and Arab worlds. Within Palazzo Cavanis, this concept manifests as a series of physical thresholds where light, shadow, noise, and ecology blur. By advancing models of knowledge grounded in hybridity, plurality, and responsiveness to context, the presentation frames exhibition-making as a vital site where diverse phenomena converge, challenge, and sustain one another. Ultimately, the collective research on display operates as an act of global dialogue — transforming individual transient observations into lasting collective insight.
‘Projects of this scale are a reminder that innovative design never happens in a vacuum. It ignites in the space between us through dialogue, through partnership, and through a willingness to see the world through someone else’s lens,’ concludes Dr. Higginbotham, Dean, VCUarts and Special Assistant to the Provost for the School of the Arts in Qatar, to designboom.

Brain scans reveal two distinct biological profiles of migraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:00:11 UTC
19:00:11 KST

A recent analysis of brain scans has revealed that people who experience migraines can be grouped into two distinct biological categories. These categories are based on how the brain is wired and physically structured, offering a new way to understand the disorder beyond traditional symptom checklists. The findings were published in the journal Cephalalgia.
Migraine is a neurological condition that causes severe head pain, sensitivity to light, and other debilitating symptoms. Doctors currently classify the disorder based on how often attacks occur and whether a patient experiences an aura, which refers to visual or sensory disturbances preceding the headache. This symptom-based approach, outlined in the International Classification of Headache Disorders, often fails to predict which treatments will work best for individual patients.
The biological differences between people with migraines remain largely unmapped. Researchers suspect that categorizing patients based on brain biology, rather than just symptom frequency, might eventually improve treatment strategies. Stanford University researchers Jaiashre Sridhar and Danielle D. DeSouza led a team to investigate whether patterns in brain imaging could identify hidden biological subgroups.
To do this, the research team used two types of magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI. Structural MRI measures the physical dimensions of the brain, such as the volume and thickness of the outer layer known as the cerebral cortex, as well as deeper subcortical structures. Functional MRI tracks blood flow to observe how different brain regions communicate when a person is at rest, a metric called functional connectivity.
The researchers first analyzed combined structural and functional brain scan data from 111 individuals with migraines and 51 healthy controls. They used a mathematical algorithm to simplify the massive amount of data and group the patients based on shared biological patterns. This exploratory approach was designed to let the data dictate the groups rather than relying on prior clinical labels.
This combined analysis identified two biological subgroups with distinct brain profiles and clinical experiences. One group tended to be older, had lived with migraines longer, and reported higher levels of daily disability. This higher-burden group also experienced longer individual headache durations and lower confidence in their ability to manage pain.
In this higher-burden group, functional MRI scans showed elevated connectivity between deeper brain structures and cortical networks responsible for attention, movement, and visual processing. Structurally, these individuals also exhibited reduced brain volume across several cortical regions, including the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, compared with the other subgroup. Many of these heightened functional connections were also elevated relative to the healthy control group.
The second subgroup presented a milder biological profile. Their brain structure was largely preserved in comparison to the first group. Their functional connectivity patterns and brain volumes were not statistically significant when compared to the healthy control group.
After identifying the combined groups, the researchers conducted a secondary analysis using only the functional connectivity data. They applied the same mathematical grouping process to see how the patients would cluster based solely on how different brain regions communicate.
This functional-only model produced two subgroups that closely matched the groups found in the initial combined analysis. Patients with higher clinical burden again clustered together, exhibiting similar patterns of elevated brain connectivity. When grouped this way, the resulting clusters did not display any differences in brain structure, indicating that functional connectivity drove most of the initial subgroupings.
Next, the team ran a third clustering model using exclusively structural MRI data. They grouped the same patients based entirely on the thickness and volume of their brain tissue.
This structural-only analysis generated two entirely different patient clusters that had almost no overlap with the groups formed by the combined or functional data. While these two new groups showed widespread differences in brain volume, they exhibited no differences in functional connectivity. This divergence indicates that structural variations represent a completely separate dimension of migraine biology than functional variations.
To verify the stability of their findings, the researchers performed a final sensitivity analysis. Instead of looking at broad functional networks, they repeated the combined analysis using a much more detailed map that divided the brain into over a hundred smaller, specific regions.
The results of this fine-grained analysis strongly mirrored the original combined model. Between 90 and 95 percent of the participants were assigned to the exact same subgroups as before. This consistency suggests that the biological groups are robust, regardless of the scale used to map the brain.
While these biological groupings provide a new perspective on migraines, the research relies on data collected at a single point in time. It is not possible to know whether prolonged migraines alter the brain over the years, or if these brain differences exist first and influence how the condition develops. The clinical differences between the two subgroups were also relatively subtle, and the groups did not align with traditional categories like chronic or episodic migraine.
The researchers noted that this was a modestly sized study, meaning the results will need to be verified in larger populations. The study also did not track the exact phase of the patients’ migraine cycle during the brain scans, such as whether they were actively having a migraine or in a resting phase. Additionally, the researchers did not account for all preventive medications the participants might have been taking at the time.
Future research will need to track larger groups of patients over extended periods to see how these biological profiles evolve and whether they can eventually guide medical care.
The study, “Neuroimaging-based subtyping of migraine identifies clinically distinct phenotypes,” was authored by Jaiashre Sridhar, Mahsa Babaei, Bharati M. Sanjanwala, Robert P. Cowan, and Danielle D. DeSouza.

The Power of Setting and Declaring a Goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

In September 2022, I set myself a very public personal goal: to run a 5-minute mile.
It was a completely mad idea. I was 58 years old, and, although in reasonably good shape, the fastest I could then complete a mile was in just over six minutes. I had given myself only eight weeks to cut around 70 seconds off my time—a massive improvement that most people familiar with running thought was unattainable.
The appeal of the mile is that it is neither a sprint nor a marathon, requiring a combination of sustained speed and endurance—strong legs, strong lungs, and mental fortitude.
In my quest, age would be a factor. The fastest known mile by a runner over 60 is 4:49, set in 2020 by 61-year-old Dan King, a former University of Colorado athlete. While I am disciplined about my exercise and run seven days a week, my training is casual in its duration and intensity—and critically, I am no athlete. Yet I would be trying to run just 11 seconds slower than the record for someone roughly my age.
I hired a coach and—to make everything transparent and public—announced my goal on LinkedIn. I also approached running experts for their opinion and advice. I encouraged followers of my LinkedIn page to engage with my journey and set stretch goals of their own.
Why would I do this? Why would I set myself up for potential failure in such a public way?
As founder and CEO of Discovery, a global financial services organization started in South Africa with the goal of making people healthier, the challenge was an opportunity to improve my own health while demonstrating the importance of physical activity and encouraging others to lace up their running shoes. Data from Vitality—a business model we pioneered for health and life insurers that tracks over 60 million life years of health and wellness data to reward positive health choices—shows this compellingly: moving from no exercise to just one physically active day per week reduces the risk of death by 36%, with positive knock-on effects for other healthy behaviors and mental wellbeing.
But most importantly, I did it out of a deep, long-standing conviction to illustrate the power of setting and declaring goals: in this case, out loud and in public. Not only would I be motivating myself, but by declaring it publicly and encouraging others to set their own goals, I hoped to spark a chain reaction.
This wasn’t just a personal ambition; it was an experiment in human motivation. Behavioral science explains why goal-setting is profoundly effective.
As rational decision makers facing options under conditions of risk and uncertainty, we think we are motivated to choose the most rational option—the one with the best combination of value and likelihood of occurring. This thinking—codified in the 1940s as “expected utility theory” by game theory founders John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern—dominated decision theory for decades.
Expected utility theory assumes a linear relationship between rival potential gains—and between potential gains and losses. But this linear model was challenged in 1979 by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. Their theory—prospect theory—proposed that losses loom larger than gains, a phenomenon known as loss aversion.
In one experiment, participants reported feeling much worse about losing $100 than they felt good about gaining $100—despite the amounts at stake being the same. A foundational reason is that people evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, typically the status quo, rather than in absolute terms. This reference point determines whether an outcome is perceived as a gain or a loss. Once a loss is perceived, loss aversion kicks in—an emotional response in which the pain of loss far outweighs the pleasure of gain. Losses are typically felt to be twice as impactful as gains of the same size.
The logic is this: by setting and declaring a goal, we put ourselves on the line. By putting something at stake, we create something to lose. And because avoiding a loss feels psychologically twice as valuable as achieving a gain, setting and declaring bold goals triggers this force, unlocking radical motivation and decisive action. By declaring a goal publicly, I created something to lose: my credibility and public accountability to my followers.
So how did my five-minute mile work out? I began, as all strenuous physical challenges should, with a health check and a baseline fitness assessment (which I also wrote about on LinkedIn). The latter gave me a cardiovascular fitness VO2 max result of 47.7, well above the 41 classified as “excellent” for men my age. My coach set me a brutal training plan, which he thought could—if all went well—slash my time by up to 30-40 seconds.
Over the next month, I stuck rigidly to my training routine. My time was improving: I managed to whittle it down to 5:40, which was stellar progress, but still a long way off from five minutes. I posted weekly “performance dashboard” updates on LinkedIn—and there, too, I saw huge gains toward my other goal of inspiring other people to set profound goals of their own. One person pledged to wrap up their PhD analysis within the year, and another set out to learn a new instrument. One of the most moving posts came from someone undergoing chemotherapy who decided to run about 3 miles in under 30 minutes—then followed up months later to say that even though it had intimidated her to set a personal goal publicly, she had achieved it.
About six weeks into my training, I got impatient. I thought, How can I run at close to 3 minutes per kilometer when I don’t train at that speed? So I pushed a little faster than my coach had suggested. Then, after my run, I went into a full-day board meeting where I sat, barely moving, for ten hours. I went home to do an easy run up a steep hill, and to my horror, I suddenly felt a sharp pain in my calf. I had torn my calf muscle.
I tried everything to fix it, including platelet-rich plasma therapy and hyperbaric oxygen therapy. I was gutted, but I had to face it: my challenge was over.
Of course, I was devastated that I didn’t achieve my goal. I had made the rookie error of going too fast too soon, and I was bitterly disappointed. But I also saw the bigger picture: I had brought my time down to 5:35, and my VO2 max had risen from 47 to 58. Nearing age 60, I was faster and fitter than I had ever been, and my running had leveled up. Moreover, people all over the world had started chasing goals of their own and sharing their progress. My 30 posts over eight weeks had reached close to 12 million people.
So, was it a success or a failure? In the final calculation, it was a success for several reasons. First, it engaged people in the importance of physical activity. Second, it proved my hypothesis: setting and declaring a goal takes you further than you would have gone without one. And third, even if you fall short of the destination, the goal—and the journey—will change you.
After my injury, one of my key takeaways was that I had nevertheless made remarkable progress as a runner. So, I set myself another goal: could I run a marathon again—something I hadn’t done in two decades—and do so at a reasonable pace, given my age? This time, I stuck to my training plan, avoided injury, and the answer was an emphatic yes.
In 2025, I ran the London Marathon in 3 hours, 37 minutes and 40 seconds, a time that put me in the top 20% of all finishers. I could never have achieved that time 20 years ago, let alone before my 2022 challenge. This had a positive knock-on effect: my result in London meant I qualified for the Boston Marathon, and I ran an even faster time in that race.
In my case, one declared goal—even a failed one—led to another. My limits expanded. And in the process, I experienced the transformative power of setting and declaring goals.
This excerpt was adapted from The Four Principles: Multiply Your Impact in Life and Leadership by Adrian Gore with permission from Macmillan Publishers.

What to Say to Someone Blasting Their Phone in Public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

There’s something uniquely irritating about being forced to listen to whatever a stranger has decided to watch on their phone. Suddenly, the airport gate has a soundtrack—and it’s a tinny succession of TikToks, action scenes, and FaceTime chatter that no one else signed up for.
As Sammie Walker Herrera, a communication coach, puts it, you might be screaming internally: “When I said I listen to all kinds of music, I didn’t mean your music.”
Still, it’s one thing to object internally—and another to ask the person to turn it down. What if they get angry, ignore you, or turn up the volume out of spite? We asked etiquette and communication experts how to make the request without turning an annoying situation into an altercation.
First, decide whether you need to say anything at all
Sometimes the easiest solution is simply to get out of earshot. Nicole Del Valle Rose, an etiquette coach and founder of the Las Vegas consultancy Poised & Proper, says the most gracious response is often the least confrontational one.
“Etiquette isn’t about correcting every behavior that bothers us,” she says. “It’s about choosing the response that creates the best outcome for everyone.”
If there’s another table open at the coffee shop or plenty of room elsewhere in the train car, relocate. You’ll solve the problem in seconds and spare both of you an awkward exchange. Save the conversation for situations where you’re truly stuck, like on a plane, in a waiting room, or aboard a packed bus.
Talk about the sound—not the person
It can be tempting to make sure the offender knows they’re being rude. Resist the urge.
“You don’t want to immediately put this person on the defensive,” says Walker Herrera, who runs Speak Y’all, a communication coaching business. “Frame how it’s impacting you, rather than that they’re doing something ‘wrong.’”
Plus, you don’t know why their phone is so loud. They might be hard of hearing, or they may not realize how far the sound is carrying. Treating it as a solvable volume problem—not evidence of a glaring character defect—makes it more likely that they’ll cooperate.
Ask a question instead of making a demand
If you’re comfortable engaging for a moment, it can help to open with a little friendliness. Larry Schooler, an assistant professor of communication studies at the University of Texas at Austin, suggests first asking what the person is listening to. After they answer, he recommends saying: “Oh, cool. I was just wondering if you could maybe lower the volume or listen to it privately; I needed to concentrate on something and was just finding it hard to do.”
Showing interest softens the interaction, Schooler says. Most people would feel uncomfortable if the first words they ever heard from a stranger were instructions to stop what they were doing or change their behavior. Giving a reason for the request also helps them understand where it’s coming from, instead of concluding that you simply dislike their music, video, or podcast.
If you’d rather skip the small talk, Michelle Retsky, a speech-language pathologist and founder of Words in Motion Therapy in New Port Richey, Fla., teaches social communication for a living. She suggests starting with a genuine question: “Excuse me, do you happen to have headphones? I’m having trouble focusing, and the sound is carrying over pretty loudly over here.”
That frames the situation as a problem the two of you can solve together, which “takes pressure off of them,” Retsky says. If they do have headphones and agree to use them, problem solved. If they don’t, follow up with: “Would you mind turning it down?”
Keep it short
There’s no need to deliver a closing argument about the deterioration of public etiquette. The longer you talk, the more uncomfortable—and potentially charged—the exchange can become.
“Short-and-to-the-point requests can be incredibly effective,” says Claudia Johnson, a licensed marriage and family therapist in Seattle. Her preferred script is just five words: “Would you mind using headphones?”
Tone matters more than finding the perfect wording. Ask politely, Johnson says, and assume the person simply didn’t realize they were bothering anyone. Most people will be happy—or at least willing—to turn down the volume.
And if they refuse? Just walk away; don’t argue or try to teach them a lesson. “We can’t change how others act; we can only ask nicely,” Johnson says. “If they say no or act immaturely about it, that says something about them and not if it was OK for you to ask.”
If the noise is making a flight, train ride, or restaurant visit genuinely unbearable, ask an employee to intervene rather than escalating the interaction yourself, Del Valle Rose suggests. And if the person seems agitated or unpredictable, skip the direct request altogether. Your peace and quiet isn’t worth jeopardizing your safety.
Above all, don’t become fixated on finding a magical combination of words that will guarantee a pleasant response. Healthy communication “doesn’t come down to saying the ‘right’ things,” Johnson says. “It’s about having the courage to say what you need in a respectful manner, while giving others the dignity of deciding how they will react.”

El Niño and Saharan Dust Silence Atlantic Hurricane Season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

It’s the middle of Atlantic hurricane season, but you’d be forgiven for forgetting that it’s even happening.
The basin has only seen three named storms since the start of hurricane season in June, a trio of weak and largely disheveled tropical storms. One or two additional tropical storms are possible through the middle of August as the season struggles against a bevy of unfavorable conditions.
They include this year’s El Niño, which is on its way to making history as sea surface temperatures soar to unprecedented heights across a critical swath of the Pacific Ocean, as well as persistent puffs of dry, dusty air that are blowing off the coast of Africa.
Together, these distant forces are working to stifle any opportunity for tropical storms to develop across the Atlantic basin. Forecasters now expect one of the quietest hurricane seasons in years, with fewer than 10 named storms likely to sneak through the unfavorable conditions.
Experts have been stunned by how fast El Niño has intensified this summer. This pattern of warmer-than-normal waters around the equator in the eastern and central Pacific significantly alters global weather patterns.
El Niño requires water temperatures in a key region around the equator to run at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal for several consecutive months. Measurements show that this swath of the Pacific is at least 1.5 degrees Celsius above average for this time of year, with portions of the region seeing astonishing anomalies of as much as 4 degrees Celsius above normal.
Abnormally warm waters in the Pacific Ocean lead to widespread pockets of rising air in the region, which alter the upper-level wind patterns. Increased convection over the Pacific, combined with the readjusted upper-level wind patterns, work together to send stronger-than-usual winds blowing east over the Atlantic basin—a phenomenon known as wind shear.
Thunderstorms are the seeds from which a tropical system grows. Strong winds aloft disrupt the structure of a budding thunderstorm, which ultimately prevents individual storms from organizing into a tropical system.
These same conditions are having the opposite impact on tropical cyclone activity across the steamy Pacific Ocean. The western Pacific typhoon season was busier by the beginning of August than any season in almost 50 years. Four storms across the region reached the equivalent strength of a Category 5 storm, including Sinlaku in April and Bavi, Dolphin, and Genevieve in July. The central and eastern Pacific are also hopping, with the US National Hurricane Center expecting above-average activity in this region through autumn.
But El Niño isn’t the only factor putting a crimp in this year’s Atlantic hurricane season this year. The West African monsoon is usually a key player in sending thunderstorms streaming over the Atlantic that can later turn into tropical systems. But this year’s monsoon has been a bit lackluster this year, with below-average rainfall in places like Sierra Leone and Guinea signaling that we’re seeing weaker disturbances than usual.
The Sahara Desert is also limiting this hurricane season’s already meager potential. Intrusions of dry, dusty air keep blowing east to west across the Atlantic, acting like a lid on the atmosphere that’s suppressing most opportunities for thunderstorm development.
Together, these factors are working together to produce the least active Atlantic hurricane season since at least 2013. Forecasters use a metric known as Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) to quantify a season based on the intensity and longevity of its storms. An average Atlantic hurricane season produces an overall ACE of 122.5. This season has so far produced an ACE of 3.1, which is just 23 percent of average for the middle of August.
Fewer storms doesn’t mean zero storms, though, and El Niño years have a history of producing intense and devastating hurricanes despite unfavorable conditions overall. Despite its struggle, this year’s Tropical Storm Arthur still may have broken Louisiana’s 24-hour rainfall record with more than 29 inches of rain reported near the community of Cottonport. And in the past, Hurricanes Camille, Ivan, Charley, Michael, Idalia, and Lee all occurred with El Niño conditions present. That means coastal residents should continue monitoring forecasts and have plans in place in case a storm does threaten land.
