17:23:15 KST

If Mali and Liel Yahalomi had decided to begin new lives in the United States, one particularly uncomfortable moment might have been avoided: video footage showing the moment police found them.
In the U.S., an adult generally has the right to leave voluntarily. If police locate an adult who has been reported missing and determine that the person is safe, left of their own free will and is not wanted in connection with a crime, officers generally cannot simply disclose that person’s whereabouts to relatives.
If the two women had told American police, “We are here voluntarily, we are healthy and we do not want anyone to know where we are,” authorities could confirm to worried relatives that they had been found safe while withholding their location. The public could receive a similar announcement so that calls and reports would stop, and, in most circumstances, that would be the end of the matter. Completely disappearing today, however, is extremely difficult, even in a country as large as the United States.
There is no precise official figure for how many Americans deliberately disappear each year, in part because voluntary departures are mixed into the much broader category of missing-person reports. Roughly 600,000 missing-person reports are filed annually in the U.S. The overwhelming majority are resolved, with people located or returning home themselves within days or weeks.
Many involve teenagers who run away or adults who temporarily cut contact with relatives. Women escaping abusive partners also account for some voluntary disappearances. Only a small proportion of cases are formally classified as abductions or involuntary disappearances, while only several thousand people remain listed as missing for more than a year.
Disappearing takes work
There was once a time when a person could leave a large East Coast city, move to a small Midwestern town and begin again with relatively little difficulty. Today, digital records, financial systems, smartphones, social media and an enormous network of surveillance and security cameras make that far harder.
There is also a crucial distinction between legally choosing to cut ties and attempting to disappear in order to evade debts, criminal proceedings or law enforcement. A person who is wanted by authorities does not gain a legal right to evade them simply by deciding to start over.
For those who are not breaking the law, a small industry has nevertheless developed around privacy, voluntary disappearance and the practical and emotional demands of leaving an old life behind. Experts disagree even on one of the most basic questions: whether someone planning to cut contact should tell one trusted person.
One argument in favor is that otherwise relatives may report the person missing, triggering a major search. But telling someone also means another person knows that the disappearance was deliberate.
Another important question is whom the person is trying to avoid. Family members have far fewer resources than governments. If someone is genuinely being sought by U.S. authorities, simply cutting personal ties is unlikely to make them unreachable.
Some specialists also emphasize the emotional side of voluntary disappearance: beginning again can require abandoning belongings, routines and connections that tie a person to their previous life.
Creating an entirely new life
“It requires a great deal of preparation,” says Jason Hanson, a former CIA officer who runs a popular YouTube channel dealing with personal security, privacy and survival. “You can’t wake up one morning and decide to disappear just because you watched a movie the night before where someone vanished within a few minutes.”
Modern life creates extensive digital traces, from social-media accounts and financial activity to phones and online services. Anyone who genuinely wants to withdraw from their old social circle must therefore understand just how much personal information is generated by ordinary daily life.
The psychological change may be just as significant. Starting over means entering a place where existing friends, acquaintances and routines no longer provide a familiar social identity. It may also mean changing habits, hobbies, appearance and the way a person presents themselves to people they meet.
The romantic Hollywood image of disappearing into a tiny town can also work against someone seeking anonymity: a newcomer may attract far more attention in a small community than in a large city where strangers arrive every day. Ultimately, voluntarily cutting all ties requires powerful reasons. It means closing a door without necessarily knowing whether it can ever be reopened.
Frank Ahearn, who has worked with people seeking greater privacy and wrote the book How to Disappear, argues that the reality bears little resemblance to movie fantasies. “You’re not simply faking your death, buying some fake documents in an alley and then retiring to a life of leisure on some small island nation,” he writes.
Disappearing legally without creating an even bigger problem than the one a person is trying to escape requires careful planning, he says. “You have to be prepared to cut contact with everyone you know, to change everything you are,” Ahearn writes.
“Disappearing means being prepared and strong enough. Otherwise, you will waste a lot of time and money trying to disappear, only to fail.”

Singaporeans urge forest protection at rally as housing plans spur concerns

Thousands of people have rallied in Singapore against plans to build homes on two forested sites in a large public display of concern over how the land-scarce city state should balance housing demand with conservation.
The projects have brought renewed urgency to a long-running debate over land use: activists say remaining mature forests should be protected, while the government says conserving more greenery would mean fewer homes for Singaporeans.
Residents, nature lovers and conservation advocates gathered at Hong Lim Park on Sunday to protest against redevelopment plans affecting Maju Forest near Clementi’s Sunset Way and the greenery around Gillman Barracks.

They chanted: “Hands off, hands off Gillman! Hands off, hands off Maju!”
Singapore’s Housing Development Board (HDB) announced last month that it planned to build homes at Clementi’s Sunset Way and Gillman Barracks, which would see the clearance of some 15 of 23 hectares (56.8 acres) of Maju forest and at least 10 hectares of the forest near Gillman.

AI generated
ROBERTVILLE, Belgium - Much-needed rain brought some respite on Aug 17 to firefighters on their fourth day battling Belgium’s worst wildfire in a century, which has scorched vast expanses of nature reserve on the German border.
Europe has been swept by weeks of devastating wildfires fuelled by dry conditions and a historically hot summer that has already contributed to the deaths of thousands of people.
France, Greece, Portugal and Spain were also battling major fires over the weekend.
In Belgium, currently the continent’s most urgent fire front, around 500 firefighters and emergency crews have mobilised to contain the blaze, which broke out on Aug 14 for reasons still unknown in the High Fens park, an area of boggy peatlands, pine forests and hiking trails.
Water-bombing aircraft and farmers’ tractors have joined forces to help tame the fire, which as of Aug 16 had spread to 3,000ha – an area half the size of Manhattan.
But Tony Hosmans, a crisis management spokesman, told reporters on Aug 17 the blaze was no longer advancing towards the German border – after creeping nearer over the weekend, prompting an evacuation order in the border town of Monschau.
The rain falling on Aug 17 on the area – with more forecast on and off throughout the week – was a welcome development.
“The wind is favourable, and the current rainfall is helping to contain the spread” of the fire, said Hosmans.
“At present, the fire is contained wherever intervention is possible,” he said – although he cautioned it had not yet been brought under control, with an aerial reconnaissance mission due to deliver a fuller picture later in the day.
The blaze broke out in an area that was ravaged by massive fires in 1911, during a similar period of heatwaves and drought.
It is the country’s largest wildfire since.
A huge area at the border has been blanketed by a thick plume of yellowish smoke, with fumes detected as far as eastern France, where authorities issued an air-pollution alert.
The smoke hazard has triggered the evacuation of two Belgian villages, whose residents were still under instruction to stay away.
‘Happening to us’
On-site operations have been made much harder by the fens’ terrain – a patchwork of heath, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy vehicles risk sinking into the ground, and firefighters struggle to tackle the fire at close range.
They have been counting heavily on aerial assistance to bring the situation under control, with two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden and two Dutch military Chinook helicopters backing up two Belgian helicopters on site.
Local farmers have also poured in to help battle the blaze, with a ballet of tractors pulling in tankers of water drawn from a nearby lake.
“We’ve provided drinks and some meals,” Annick Dodemont, who runs one of many local businesses supporting the firefighting operation, told AFP.
“We can’t go up there ourselves, so we help however we can,” said the 41-year-old.
Like much of Europe, Belgium has experienced a new spell of intense heat and drought in recent days.
Temperatures reached as high as 37 deg C in some parts of the country on Aug 14, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks.
“It’s pretty shocking,” Dodemont said from her restaurant in Eupen. “You always think it happens somewhere else. Well, not anymore. It’s happening to us.” AFP

Two acquaintances of Klepach told the independent Russian news outlet The Bell about his dismissal. One source said VEB.RF head Igor Shuvalov fired Klepach after a “call from above.” A second source confirmed that the dismissal was linked to Klepach’s May speech.

The Bell sent VEB.RF an inquiry but had not received a response as of publication.
The day before, the independent Russian news outlet The Moscow Times drew attention to remarks Klepach made at a meeting of the Nikitsky Club at the Moscow Exchange in late May 2026, where he said the Ukrainian economy, “despite everything, is surviving.” “So we will not win this competition in the war of attrition. We have an illusion that everything will collapse there [in Ukraine]. It hasn’t collapsed, and it won’t. Our costs are growing,” he said. Klepach also said Russia is losing “both the technological and economic competition in the world,” and not “only to China and the U.S.,” but “in some ways” to Ukraine as well.
Klepach, 67, spent 12 years as VEB.RF’s chief economist after a decade at the Economic Development Ministry. Alexandra Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Berlin Center, said that Klepach “was never afraid to defend his opinion.” “One need only recall his public clashes with Alexei Ulyukaev in 2011 and his departure from the Economic Development Ministry, where Klepach was responsible for macroeconomic forecasting, when Ulyukaev became minister,” she recalled.

EU to propose tougher sanctions on Russia this autumn, Kaja Kallas says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:19:59 UTC
17:19:59 KST

The EU is to propose more “far-reaching” sanctions against Russia this autumn after the bloc’s latest package was watered down amid pressure to protect national economic interests.
The European Union's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc will seek tougher sanctions on Russia this autumn, signalling a fresh push to ramp up pressure on Moscow.
In an interview with German newspaper Die Welt, Kallas said that in the coming months she would "put forward the most far-reaching sanctions listings since the start of the war", adding that the listings would raise the total number of sanctioned Russian companies and individuals "by a third".
"The pressure must keep growing until Moscow ends its war," she added.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion against Ukraine in 2022, the EU has approved 21 packages of sanctions targeting Russian political and military leaders, businessmen, oligarchs and companies.
Over 3000 individuals and entities have been sanctioned so far, with more than €28 billion in private assets in the EU frozen.
Kallas' comments suggest that the upcoming sanctions could see a further 1000 individuals and entities targeted. Any listing must secure the unanimous approval of all 27 EU member states.
The sanctions also aim to restrict Moscow's ability to fund and sustain its operations in Ukraine, by targeting its military complex, industrial base and export operations.
Kallas said that the Kremlin had "already paid a high price for the EU sanctions", estimating the economic cost to be at over one trillion euros.
Yet, recent attempts to broaden the scope of EU sanctions on Russia have been met with surprising resistance from some member states.
The most recent, 21st package of sanctions on Russia was almost derailed by Greece, which insisted on a special exemption from an EU-wide ban on the shipment of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) as a precondition to approving the sanctions.
Athens ultimately secured the exemption despite other diplomats' outrage, raising major questions over the way national economic interests could take precedence over the appetite to inflict deeper economic pain on Russia.
Kallas also expressed optimism that the US and the EU could "move closer" in their sanctions policy, after a Russia sanctions bill championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham was passed in the senate in a bipartisan vote.
There has been mounting anxiety in Brussels over the eroding of financial support to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia since Donald Trump's re-election.

Spain extradited state registrar to Ukraine after nearly four years in hiding
Kyiv • UNN
The man is suspected of illegally registering a deceased person's apartment, causing losses of UAH 1 million. He was extradited from Spain and taken into custody.
Spain extradited a state registrar to Ukraine over the illegal registration of an apartment, the Prosecutor General’s Office reported on Monday, UNN writes.
With the participation of the Prosecutor General’s Office and the Zaporizhzhia Regional Prosecutor’s Office, and in cooperation with the competent authorities of the Kingdom of Spain, a state registrar who had been hiding from investigators since 2022 was extradited to Ukraine
According to the investigation, "in May 2021, in order to obtain an undue benefit, he used a forged court decision and unlawfully registered ownership of a three-room apartment in the name of a local resident."
"The apartment’s owner died without any heirs. Under the law, the property was to pass into the ownership of the territorial community of Zaporizhzhia as escheated property and become part of the city’s housing stock. Instead, ownership was registered in the name of a woman who identified herself as the deceased’s cohabitant. As a result of the unlawful actions, the territorial community suffered almost UAH 1 million in damages," the prosecutor’s office stated.
In September 2022, the state registrar was notified in absentia that he was suspected under Part 3 of Article 365-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. He was subsequently placed on the international wanted list.
"On August 10, 2026, the suspect was handed over to the Ukrainian side at the "Krakivets - Korchova" border crossing point. On August 12, the court ordered his detention without setting bail," the prosecutor’s office stated.

Lithuanian firefighters return from wildfire mission in southern France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:17:00 UTC
17:17:00 KST

Forty Lithuanian firefighters returned home Sunday after a two-week mission helping French authorities battle wildfires in southern France.
The Perkūnas team was deployed to the Bordeaux and Marseille regions, where it worked alongside French and other international crews to conduct reconnaissance, extinguish smouldering hotspots and prevent fires from reigniting.
Mission commander Dalius Kunigėlis said the team returned “tired but motivated” after helping suppress forest fires and protect settlements from the flames.
“I think it was a great experience,” Kunigėlis told reporters. “During the journey back, we had time to discuss what we can present to our leadership and share our expertise. [...] Tactical details may differ slightly, but the core principle is the same – to save and help people.”
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the mission demonstrated Lithuania’s solidarity with other European countries and the readiness of its emergency personnel to assist during disasters.
He said Lithuanian firefighters are valued for their training, equipment and ability to carry out international relief missions.
Kęstutis Agintas, deputy director of the Fire and Rescue Department, said the experience gained in France would be valuable for future operations. Lithuanian firefighters have previously taken part in international relief efforts following earthquakes and floods, as well as wildfire suppression missions.
About 20 teams from other countries assisted French authorities during the latest wildfire emergency, Agintas said. The Lithuanian contingent operated as one of the ground teams.
The wildfires in southern France forced about 220,000 people to evacuate. More than 200 homes were destroyed and about 42,000 hectares of land were burned.
The Lithuanian firefighters were deployed through the European Union’s Civil Protection Mechanism. It was the sixth international aid mission involving Lithuanian firefighters since 2010.

Beloved US actress Hayden Panettiere, best known for her roles in the TV shows Heroes, Nashville as well as the Scream films, has died aged 36.
Her father Skip Panettiere described her as an “incredible light and a force of nature.”
He said in a statement via The Hollywood Reporter: “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen. We ask for privacy as our family takes time to process this unimaginable loss.”
The cause of her death was not immediately available. TMZ reports that Panettiere flew out of LA the day before her death with on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson.
“Police responded to an incident involving Hayden today and there is currently an open investigation,” South Carolina police said.
Panettiere, who would have turned 37 on Friday, began her career as a child actor, and was just four years old when she appeared on US soap opera One Life To Live. She then made her film debut at nine years old, voicing a young ant called Dot in Pixar's 1998 film A Bug's Life.
Her breakout role came when she starred as cheerleader Claire Bennet in the superhero series Heroes in 2006. She went on to play Juliette Barnes in Nashville and then fan favourite Kirby Reed in Scream 4 in 2011 and Scream VI in 2023.

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- Hurricane Lala damaged homes, bridges and power infrastructure across Hawaii over the weekend, leaving more than 250,000 people without electricity after the storm weakened to a tropical storm early Sunday.
At least 100 homes were damaged in southern Hawaii Island, commonly known as the Big Island, with several occupied homes reportedly swept off their foundations by flash floods, Hawaii Governor Josh Green said Sunday.
Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda said an aerial assessment found six bridges destroyed or significantly damaged in the Kau district, leaving the community of Pahala isolated by road. County officials also reported road damage, flooded buildings and debris across the Kau district.
Search-and-rescue teams used Hawaii National Guard high-water vehicles and a U.S. Coast Guard helicopter to reach residents stranded by flooding, Hawaii County said. An ambulance crew was evacuated after floodwaters pushed its vehicle against a guardrail in the Pahala area.
Hawaiian Electric said more than 250,000 customers remained without power at 11 a.m. Sunday (GMT 2100) across Hawaii Island, Maui County and Oahu. The utility warned that outages could last weeks or even months in the hardest-hit rural areas because of damage to transmission infrastructure and limited access.
Governor Green said at least three hospitals were operating on backup generators.
Authorities were investigating whether any reported deaths were linked to the storm. A man was killed in a traffic crash on Saturday, while a body was found near a stream on Oahu, but officials said it was unclear whether either death was storm-related.
Several schools on Hawaii Island were also closed because of storm damage and unsafe road conditions, according to the Hawaii State Department of Education.
The U.S. National Weather Service said exceptional rainfall struck parts of the Big Island, with nearly 900 mm reported at some higher-elevation sites.
One of its meteorologists Robert Ballard told National Public Radio Sunday that the rainfall amount brought by Lala was beyond what the island can normally absorb. Ballard said Lala intensified as it approached the Big Island over unusually warm ocean water, which he described as relatively rare.
Lala weakened to a tropical storm early Sunday after passing just south of the Big Island. The Hawaii Emergency Management Agency urged residents to stay off roads, warning that flooding, fallen trees and downed power lines remained hazards. ■

MANILA, Aug. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Philippine government has suspended in-person classes in Metro Manila and 12 other provinces as heavy rains from tropical cyclones and the southwest monsoon continue to batter the country, local media reported on Monday.
According to Memorandum Circular No. 127 issued by the presidential office on Monday, schools and government agencies in affected areas were directed to adopt alternative work arrangements, except for frontline services such as health, disaster response and other essential functions.
At least 50 cities and towns have declared a state of calamity, with Pampanga and Cavite placing all their municipalities under the status, according to the Office of Civil Defense.

US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to push a 15-point Gaza plan Israel has rejected.
The meeting on Monday comes a day after Kushner’s visit to El-Alamein, Egypt, to convene with Qatari, Turkish and Egyptian mediators. He was accompanied by Board of Peace Director-General Nickolay Mladenov and former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair.

Kushner also held a rare meeting with members of the Hamas group’s political leadership, “with the objective of translating the roadmap’s obligations into concrete, verifiable steps”, an official familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera.
In late July, Trump said an agreement had been reached for the disarmament of Hamas. The deal was credited to the US-led Board of Peace, inaugurated in February 2026 and including roughly 40 countries – including Israel and several Arab states, though no Palestinian representatives – with Trump installed as its chair for life.
Netanyahu, who is seeking re-election in October, has publicly rejected the plan, objecting to a provision under which Hamas would gradually disarm and hand over governance of the strip to an international force in exchange for Israeli forces withdrawing from Gaza.

The Board of Peace was set up under a broader Gaza “ceasefire” reached between Israel and Hamas in late 2025. At least 1,260 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza by Israel since the ceasefire took effect.

Several devotees were reportedly injured after a stampede-like situation broke out near temple complex
NEW DELHI: Several devotees were reportedly injured after a stampede-like situation broke out near the Mahakaleshwar Temple complex in Madhya Pradesh's Ujjain on Monday, amid a massive crowd gathered for Nag Panchami and Sawan Somvar.The incident was reported near Harsiddhi Chauraha after a rumour about electric current in barricades triggered panic among devotees heading towards the Shri Nagchandreshwar Temple, according to ANI. Some barricades reportedly broke as the crowd surged, leaving several devotees injured.The injured were taken to Charak Hospital for treatment, while Ujjain Collector and Superintendent of Police reached the spot and took charge of the situation.However, the temple administration denied that any chaos or stampede had occurred inside the temple and said devotees were continuing to have darshan without disruption.Temple administration denies stampedeMahakal Temple administrator Pratham Kaushik told ANI that darshan at the Nagchandreshwar Temple was continuing smoothly despite the unusually large crowd."On the occasion of Nag Panchami, darshan at Nag Chandreshwar Mandir at Shri Mahakaleshwar Mandir is continuously going on...So,
it is important to clarify that no chaos or any such incident has occurred at the temple. All devotees are having darshan at the temple seamlessly. Due to Nag Panchami and Sawan Somvar today, a massive number of devotees had darshan today. Till 12 noon today, more than 6 lakh devotees had darshan of Bhagwan Nag Chandreshwar and more than 2 lakh devotees had darshan of Lord Shri Mahakaleshwar. All devotees have been provided every possible facilities by the temple administration. Darshan continues at the temple."The temple administration said the large turnout was linked to Nag Panchami coinciding with Monday during the holy month of Shravan.The Nagchandreshwar Temple, located atop the Mahakaleshwar Temple, opens only once a year for 24 hours on the occasion of Nag Panchami. Thousands of devotees gather to seek the blessings of Lord Nagchandreshwar during the annual opening.Devotees report injuries near Harsiddhi ChaurahaWhile the temple administration denied any incident inside the temple, reports emerged of devotees being injured in the area around Harsiddhi Chauraha.A woman whose son was admitted to hospital told ANI that he was injured after being caught under a barricade while heading towards the temple."This occurred at Harsiddhi Chauraha. He came under a barricade when he was going for a darshan at Nath Chandreshwar Mandir. A stampede had broken out there. Nobody helped him. Only one man carried him here..." she said.One of the injured, Sagar, said he had been waiting in the queue for several hours before the incident occurred."I was in the queue at Mahakal Mandir for the darshan. After seven to eight hours, I reached Harsiddhi Chauraha. We stood there for two hours. The crowd was swelling and since it was time for the aarti, we were stopped there. Suddenly, the barricades were opened and a stampede broke out," he said.
He said he was trapped and injured after the barricades collapsed."The tent fell, and all the barricades fell too. Both of my legs were caught under the barricade. One of my legs is fractured. The arrangements were really poor at the temple. Nobody helped me. Only one man came and helped me; he carried me to a health camp, from where I was taken away in an ambulance," Sagar was quoted as saying by news agency ANI.Chaos was also reported near Bada Ganesh Temple, Neelkanth Square and along the route from Kark Raj Parking towards the Harsiddhi entrance.Officials subsequently reached the affected areas and worked to restore order as devotees continued to arrive at the temple complex.The incident occurred amid one of the year's biggest religious gatherings in Ujjain, with the simultaneous observance of Nag Panchami and Sawan Somvar drawing lakhs of devotees to the Mahakaleshwar temple.

Belgian demand pushes Dutch coal plants to run harder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:08:59 UTC
17:08:59 KST

Belgian demand pushes Dutch coal plants to run harder
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch coal-fired power stations have generated more electricity so far this year than in the whole of 2024, driven by high gas prices and a sharp rise in demand from Belgium, the Financieele Dagblad reported on Monday.
Coal plants normally run harder from October, when electricity demand rises and less wind and solar power is available.
The figures come from data platform Nationaal Energie Dashboard. Coal was last burned at this rate during the 2022 gas crisis, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine pushed gas prices so high that coal became the cheaper fuel.
Belgian shortfall
 Much of the extra output has left the country. Belgium took its last two working nuclear reactors offline, which went offline in April for safety upgrades.
That left Belgium importing 7.5 billion kWh more electricity than it exported in the second quarter, a record, beating a previous high set in late 2015. Most of it came from the Netherlands and France.
“Coal plants are also stepping in,” energy transition specialist Martien Visser at Hanze University of Applied Sciences in Groningen told broadcaster NOS, “because demand for electricity from abroad has increased.”
Climate trade-off
 Visser said the extra Dutch emissions were not necessarily bad news, because European rules cap total emissions across member states, so higher output in one country can mean less elsewhere.
“Not all countries are moving at the same speed on the energy transition,” he told NOS, adding that Dutch coal was preferable to German lignite, which is dirtier. Burning coal also frees up gas – 60 million cubic metres a week, or around 20% of Dutch demand.
Coal is the most polluting way to generate electricity, and Dutch law requires the three remaining plants, two on the Maasvlakte near Rotterdam and one in the Eemshaven, to stop burning it by 2030.
CDA leader Henri Bontenbal called earlier this year for the plants to stay open as a backstop.

Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing departs for Russia to expand energy and economic ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:07:51 UTC
17:07:51 KST

Myanmar junta chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing left for Russia on Monday for his first official visit to the country since he assumed the presidency in April, according to state media.
Russia will be the fifth country Min Aung Hlaing has visited since becoming president, with official trips to India, China, Laos, and, earlier this month, Thailand.
The former general is the subject of a raft of Western sanctions and has been on a quest for international legitimacy since winning a vote in parliament to become president, which came after an election dominated by an army-backed party in the absence of a viable opposition.
Min Aung Hlaing made four visits to Russia as junta chief, the first in June 2021 to attend a security conference, five months after seizing power in a coup. He visited twice in 2022 and again in March 2025, when he held formal talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Russia is hoping to open up opportunities in Myanmar for its energy companies. The two countries signed an agreement to construct a small-scale nuclear power plant in Myanmar when Min Aung Hlaing met Putin in 2025.
Russia, Myanmar strengthening defense ties
Russia and Myanmar signed a memorandum on investment cooperation for the strategically located Dawei Special Economic Zone in February 2025, including the construction of a port and an oil refinery.
Min Aung Hlaing's latest trip includes a Myanmar-Russia business forum. Joining him will be the chief minister of the Tanintharyi region, where Dawei is located, and the head of Myanmar's aerospace agency, according to state media.
Defense ties have grown in recent years, with Moscow providing army training and university scholarships to thousands of Myanmar soldiers, as well as selling arms to a military blacklisted by some Western countries.
Russia also said earlier this year that it would help train Myanmar's first cosmonaut.

Likud internal primaries begin as tensions continue over Netanyahu's expanded slate controls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:07:26 UTC
17:07:26 KST

The Likud Party closed its polling stations for its internal primaries on Monday evening after approximately 140,000 registered members were eligible to vote for candidates seeking spots on the party’s Knesset slate ahead of the October 27 elections.
The primaries came amid fierce internal tensions over changes that have expanded chairman Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s control over the party’s Knesset slate, which have made the primaries more competitive than in past years.
The voter turnout reached 53.5%, with 76,068 party members voting in the primaries, up about ten percentage points from the primaries held four years ago, taking into account the difference in voting hours, the Likud stated.
The results are expected to be announced late on Monday night.
Candidates who receive realistic slots on the list could hold significant roles in the government if Netanyahu is to be elected as prime minister in the October 27 election.
The polling began at 10 a.m. and continued until 9 p.m. at stations throughout the country.
The over 100 candidates seeking to secure a slot on the party's list continued to campaign throughout the morning. Many posted pictures of themselves with Netanyahu, such as Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, who is expected to receive a high slot on the list.
Regional Cooperation Minister David Amsalem posted a photo of himself voting, calling on registered members to join.
"I believe in Likud members, in their wisdom, their hearts, and in our path. We did our part with great love. Now I call on everyone who has not yet voted: Get out of the house, go to the polls, and make your voice heard," he stated.
Likud ministers and members of Knesset running in the primaries also continued throughout the day to photograph themselves casting their ballots at the various voting stations throughout the country.
Regional Cooperation Minister David Amsalem posted a photo of himself voting, calling on registered members to join.
"I believe in Likud members, in their wisdom, their hearts, and in our path. We did our part with great love. Now I call on everyone who has not yet voted: Get out of the house, go to the polls, and make your voice heard," he stated.
Parties not required to hold primaries, Likud holds votes
Netanyahu showed up at the Jerusalem polling station at the International Convention Center (ICC) to vote in the afternoon.
He stated on Sunday ahead of the primaries that he would join the voting and cast his ballot “for a winning slate.”
“I trust you, Likud members, to choose your representatives correctly, according to your own judgment. I am not interfering in the national list, and I wish everyone success,” Netanyahu added.
Agriculture and Food Security Minister Avi Dichter told The Jerusalem Post, while at the ICC in Jerusalem to cast his vote, that this year’s primaries had generated a different level of enthusiasm, with turnout among members appearing “higher and stronger,” and voters arriving with “a wide smile on their face.”
Giving backing to the premier amid the tensions over the reserved slots, Dicter added that "we need to build a good team beside and behind Prime Minister Netanyahu."
It was later reported by Israeli media that haredi (ultra-Orthodox) activists had registered to the party ahead of the primaries to vote in favor of preferred candidates, despite not having a previous connection to the party.
Likud has for years prided itself on conducting primaries in which its registered members are eligible to vote for the Knesset list. Parties are not required to hold primaries in Israel, and only a few do so.
Netanyahu pushed to change the system in recent weeks ahead of the primaries, leading to an especially competitive race with even fewer slots available than usual.
Netanyahu was granted the authority to determine eight slots within the first 30 spots on the party list last month following a vote on the controversial decision by the Likud Central Committee.
There were reports that Netanyahu had threatened to leave Likud if the proposed changes were not advanced.
Those within the party who oppose changing the primaries have argued that it will cause those who would otherwise score highly in the primaries to fall further down the list.
The Likud primaries are further competitive because the party currently has around 40 ministers and MKs serving in the government and Knesset, but recent polls project the party winning only about 22 seats, leaving many at risk of losing their places on the party’s Knesset list.
Further tensions surrounding the slots also come after the Tel Aviv District Court last week rejected Likud MK Afif Abed’s attempt to restore a narrowly approved change allowing current and former MKs, ministers and deputy ministers to run in the party’s district primaries, leaving the restrictions in place ahead of the vote.
Likud had announced last week that one of Netanyahu’s first reserved slots would go to entrepreneur and businessman Oren Dobronsky.
Additional reserved slots were later granted by Netanyahu to three ministers: Defense Minister Israel Katz, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, and Likud Central Committee Chairman Haim Katz, who also holds multiple ministerial portfolios.
The party said its internal court ruled that the defense minister should receive a reserved slot in order to “allow him to focus on security needs rather than engage in politics at this time.”
Sa'ar to receive reserved slot as part of party merger
Likud also stated that Sa’ar would receive a reserved slot as part of the merger agreement between his party and Likud and that the Likud Central Committee chairperson would receive a slot due to his senior position in the party.
Sa’ar had announced in 2025 that his New Hope-United Right would be merging with Likud, and would be returning to the party. He previously resigned from Likud in 2020, heavily criticizing Netanyahu at the time.
The changes to the party’s primaries that have expanded Netanyahu’s control over the Knesset list have led to fierce internal tensions, with some party members in favor and others strongly against.
A fierce critic of changing the system has been MK Tally Gotliv, who is viewed as a candidate who would receive broad support from registered party members.
She claimed during the voting that there were polling stations with fake ballots that did not include her name.
"Stay alert. Likud activists and vote contractors are in a panic over the power of independent votes," she stated.
"Update me directly. A polling station with a fake ballot will be disqualified," she added.
Gotliv has sharply criticized the Tuesday decision to reserve the slots for the three ministers, condemning the defense minister.
She called the decision to grant the defense minister a reserved slot “a disgraceful move that mocks Likud voters."
Likud MK Amit Halevi, who has expressed support for allowing the premier to reserve slots, told the Post on Sunday that the primaries “will be a democratic celebration in the Likud.”
“I wish more parties conducted themselves democratically like the Likud. Some 140,000 members, active, engaged citizens who make their voices heard and have an influence, will go to the polls tomorrow,” he added.
The primaries determine the Likud’s Knesset slate, with the party chairman placed first. Registered members then vote for candidates on the national list, while members from geographic districts vote for candidates from their respective districts.
Candidates chosen on the national list are combined with district representatives and places that guarantee representation for groups including women, immigrants, young members, and minorities. The regulations also reserve certain positions for candidates chosen by the party chairman.
The precise locations of those different categories are determined before each election through the party’s temporary election regulations. That is why the current fight has centered not only on whether primaries will take place, but on how much of the resulting slate the members will actually control.
Other party leaders from Netanyahu's coalition expressed support for the primaries.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who leads the far-Right Otzma Yehudit Party, voiced his support for various Likud candidates, including Gotliv and Women's Advancement Minister May Golan.
The Religious Zionist Party, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, also expressed support.
"Good luck to all the candidates, and, God willing, success to all of us together in the upcoming elections," the party stated.
"The national camp must continue to lead Israel toward continued growth and prosperity," it added.
Democrats Party leader Yair Golan, from the oppostion bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu in the upcoming elections. sharply criticized the primaries.
"Never have so many people vied for a place on the deck of the Titanic," he stated.
Sam Halpern and Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

Japan tracks four Russian missile boats passing close to its coast off Hokkaido

Japan's Self-Defense Forces shadowed four Russian missile boats as they passed close to the country's northern coast, the Japanese Joint Staff reported. The warships never entered Japanese waters, yet the move sharpened a diplomatic standoff over islands Russia seized in 1945. Tokyo lodged a protest and summoned Russia's ambassador.
Japan tracked the warships back through the strait
On 14 August, Japan's Maritime Self-Defense Force spotted the four boats near Cape Soya on Hokkaido, heading west. A P-3C patrol aircraft from the 2nd Air Wing watched them and gathered information. The boats stayed 40 kilometers from shore and did not cross into Japanese waters.
The vessels carried hull numbers 916, 946, 971, and 978. Japan had spotted the same four ships on 9 August, 70 kilometers northwest of Rebun Island. They then passed east through the Soya Strait before doubling back.
The transit followed Putin's trip to a contested island
The return passage came days after Vladimir Putin visited Iturup—one of the Kuril Islands—on 13 August. The Soviet Union seized the island in 1945, breaking a neutrality pact it had signed with Japan. Moscow treats the Kuril archipelago as strategically vital and keeps building up forces there. Iturup hosts the Burevestnik military airfield.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called Putin's trip absolutely unacceptable. She said it contradicts Tokyo's stance on the Northern Territories, as Japan calls the islands. Japan's Foreign Ministry summoned Russia's ambassador, Nikolai Nozdrev, and lodged a firm protest. It asked him to pass Tokyo's position to Moscow at once.
What the Molniya-1 missile boats carry
Militarnyi noted that the project 12411M Molniya-1 boats, which NATO calls Tarantul III, come from the Almaz Central Marine Design Bureau. The first entered service in 1981.
They are built to hit surface targets in coastal and near-sea zones. Their main upgrade over earlier versions was four supersonic Moskit anti-ship missiles, replacing the older Termit.
Each boat can reach 41 knots and carries a crew of 40. Its weapons include a 76mm gun, two rapid-fire 30mm mounts, and Igla-1 air-defense missiles.
The four belong to Russia's Pacific Fleet. The oldest, hull 971, entered service in 1990, and the newest, hull 916, in 2003.

Exclusive: Brussels keen to monitor UFOs under the radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:06:04 UTC
17:06:04 KST

Brussels has signalled it is monitoring unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) and has hinted at improving capabilities, according to documents seen by Euronews.
The European Commission seems to have been monitoring unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) under the radar since at least 2023, according to a document from the Commission's defence department seen by Euronews, which pertains to sky and space observations in Malaysia.
"We are getting better at seeing it (UAPs) and better identifying it as our technological capacities improve, but we need to get even better," the letter read, signalling the EU executive is actively monitoring the phenomenon more than officially stated and seems keen to investigate it.
Formerly known as unidentified flying objects (UFOs), the term UAP was introduced by the United States defence department, the Pentagon, in August 2020, when Washington established the UAP Task Force to investigate inexplicable occurrences in restricted airspace.
The topic took on a more serious tone after a New York Times report revealed in 2017 that the US defence department files contained UAP footage from military flights that the US Navy had released.
Euronews also identified a Malaysian father and son — amateur astronomers internationally recognised by space agencies for their discoveries of the surfaces and activities on the moon in 2020 — who reached out to the Commission with a letter titled "UAP captures in the airspace and deep space using our UV infrared telescope" in October 2022.
The family duo sent 37 sky and space footage images to the Commission, including alleged UAPs, and asked President Ursula von der Leyen about their origins.
They noted that "all governments simply have no opinions" of these UAPs when confronted about them, and said they appear to be flying "very near to aircraft and important targets, such as military and nuclear facilities".
"We have also detected various signals from up above through the local networks Wi-Fi frequency," the Malaysian duo wrote.
Since these UAPs were spotted over Malaysia, the Commission would have no authority to investigate the matter, the EU executive responded.
However, the Commission said it would propose to its 27 member states to "increase its ability to detect objects in the space environment around the Earth".
"This is partly to help us better identify the UAPs that you have seen and the many pieces of space debris that endanger the many uses of space," the Commission said.
"We do not claim that in the future this will solve all cases like those you have reported, but maybe some of them."
The Malaysian amateur astronomers also reached out to NASA, the director general of the Malaysian Nuclear Agency, Abdul Rahim Harun, the Malaysian Ministry of Science, Technology & Innovation and the Canadian Defense Ministry. All entities politely shunned the appeal.
Former Canadian MP Larry Maguire, who was also approached individually by the Malaysians, encouraged the pair.
"I suspect that more and more people around the world will be turning their attention to the skies and will be collecting even more data and recordings in the coming year," Maguire wrote in an email in June 2022, seen by Euronews.
"At the end of the day, the skies aren't classified, and as more information is collected, it will lead to more public awareness of the issue."
US landmark Congress hearing
A landmark US Congress UAP hearing, hosted by the House Oversight Committee's National Security Subcommittee, took place on 26 July 2023. The hearing focused on national security implications and explosive allegations of classified government programmes that retrieve and reverse-engineer UAPs, according to the US government.
The change in designation, from UFO to UAP, was meant to kill the stigma associated with UFOs and more exotic theories that have circulated for decades, and to widen the scope of the phenomena.
In the EU, discussions about the topic remain limited and subject to stigma. This starkly contrasts with countries such as the US, which has released several confidential files in recent years. Most recently, it established a UAP Science Council chaired by Avi Loeb, a theoretical physicist who specialises in astrophysics and cosmology at Harvard University.
France is the only EU country with a dedicated, state-funded UAP monitoring and investigation centre: the Study Group and Information on Non-Identified Aerospace Phenomena, more commonly known as GEIPAN.
Since its inception in 1977, GEIPAN has analysed over 3,300 UAP cases. Exactly 106 investigations have been classified as unexplained after thorough analysis. Another 1,014 cases are unresolved due to insufficient data to conduct a proper investigation.
On 29 June, the French Parliament held a major discussion on UAPs. The debate centred on UAP research, work on UAPs by GEIPAN and the French Air and Space Force, and potentially liaising with the US to garner “responses from public authorities”.
“We want to move beyond sensationalism and fantasies and instead address, in a serious and rational way, an issue that is generating significant interest,” French MP Arnaud Saint-Martin, who has a background in aerospace and astronautics, told Le Parisien.
Flight safety concerns
Over the past decades, several EU lawmakers have questioned the Commission about the phenomena, more recently raising flight safety concerns as reports of pilot sightings increase.
These safety concerns gained momentum after several US congressional hearings featured testimony from military pilots describing "unexplainable" flying behaviour that defied the laws of physics.
In 2025 and 2026, MEP Fabio De Masi (Germany/Non-attached) asked the Commission several times to review and update EU aviation reporting systems to introduce a dedicated and standardised reporting category for UAP incidents. This would ensure consistency, data integrity and higher standards of flight safety across EU countries.
The plea has also been raised by pilots who argue that the lack of standardised reporting protocols for UAP encounters hampers data collection and risk mitigation.
They argue that sudden appearances of UAPs may lead to a loss of situational awareness or to emergency manoeuvres, fearing that the phenomena could temporarily cause malfunctions in aircraft sensors and communication systems.
Rob Akkermans, a commercial pilot working for a Dutch airline, spoke to Euronews about his experiences over the past 35 years. The first was in the early 1990s and the last two in 2023 and 2024.
"We, two pilots and four cabin crew members, were on a flight in 2023 from the Middle East to the Netherlands. For over two hours, starting around 19:30 UTC, we witnessed this strange phenomenon, which we found truly remarkable," Akkermans told Euronews, noting that all six crew members viewed the scene from the cockpit.
"It began while we were south of Cyprus. Precisely on a heading of 300 degrees (Magnetic North) — at an elevation of roughly 25 to 30 degrees and at a very high altitude — we saw a light flare up intensely and then slowly fade out. Subsequently, this occurred more frequently, often accompanied by one or two other lights that would also flare up and fade," the Dutchman explained.
"The most bizarre aspect was that one of the three lights would sometimes manoeuvre around the others. It resembled a chase — what air forces call 'dogfighting' — after which two or all three of them would fade out again," he said.
"Initially, we thought it might be a mission over the Balkans, but upon reaching the Balkans, we witnessed the same spectacle — still on the same heading, at the same angle, and at a very high altitude. After approximately 21:30 UTC, the lights suddenly vanished with incredible speed, and we did not see it again," he added.
Akkermans said that the following day, one of his colleagues witnessed the same from his back garden in the Netherlands.
The Dutch pilot said that after his experiences, he felt "a mix of wonder and surprise because what I saw was completely unexplainable," saying that such an experience "never truly leaves you".
But that excitement quickly turned into a distraction during the flight.
"Emotionally, the worrying part to deal with was frustration and concern over the stigma. You are forced to carry this experience in silence, worrying far more about the professional consequences of the taboo than the actual safety risk you just witnessed," he said.
Christiaan van Heijst, 43, a Boeing 747 captain with over 20 years of commercial flying experience, shared with Euronews four experiences he had between 2005 and 2010. Two of them were particularly noteworthy.
His second sighting, in Greece in 2005, probably on the island of Mykonos, was late in the evening.
"After landing at night, we made a 180° turn on the runway, and during the turn we saw a bright light appearing in the sky at extremely high altitude. It moved instantly, disappeared, appeared again, moved roughly the same distance, disappeared again — about three times," the Dutch pilot told Euronews.
"Before it appeared roughly two times that distance and instantly shot off at instant and unbelievable speed, without acceleration: just instant speed and it was gone from sight."
Van Heijst noted that the US Carrier Strike Group 2 with the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier was passing by in the Mediterranean on its way to the Persian Gulf that night for the Second Gulf War.
"This was mentioned in airspace closure (NOTAMS) as well (...) Unknown if these events are connected," van Heijst said.
His fourth sighting took place during a flight with a 737 from Amsterdam to Málaga in the late afternoon of 23 January 2010.
"We noticed a certain object far ahead of us showing a rounded rectangular shape as if we were looking in the rear side of a contrail. But we were flying at 41,000 feet and there is hardly any commercial and/or military traffic above us at these altitudes," van Heijst said.
"While still flying in the north of Spain, we asked Madrid Air Traffic Control if there was any known traffic ahead and above us. They told us there was no traffic at all, and wondered why we asked. So, we told them we saw an object far ahead of us and rather large," he added.
"We were just casually wondering what it was. He immediately asked us to contact the military air traffic control frequency and tell them what we saw. Military air traffic control was prompt, interested and took serious note of all we saw," the Dutch pilot continued.
"Military air traffic control confirmed there was no other traffic at all, all the way down to Morocco — no military activity, no commercial traffic, no weather balloons, nothing. We saw the stationary object all the time for an hour at least, until we descended into the clouds over Málaga, far to the south of the Iberian peninsula," he added.
While van Heijst said he felt "no emotional response to any of those sightings", he emphasised that if something is present in the airspace and authorities are unable to identify it, then "first and foremost it is a safety issue and not science fiction".
Joachim Dekkers is the founder and chairperson of the UAP Coalition Netherlands, a foundation that supports professionals who have encountered UAP. He said the greatest threat to European flight safety is the silence caused by stigma. This means that 90% of pilot sightings go unreported.
"Without a dedicated UAP category in aviation safety systems, flight crews are forced to misclassify critical data. The EU cannot maintain global leadership in aviation safety while ignoring a reality other major powers measure," Dekkers told Euronews.
"We must normalise UAP reporting across member states to guarantee total sovereignty and airspace transparency."
Although no conclusive evidence links UAPs to foreign adversaries, the possibility that some UAPs represent advanced espionage technology, such as drones, cannot be dismissed.
But MEP De Masi countered this argument. He said that neither the EU Commission nor the Council claims to possess specific evidence on the origin of these airspace incursions.
"This is quite astonishing given surveillance of airspace and critical infrastructure. Either our airspace is vulnerable, and we have a major flight safety and security risk, or the EU is misleading public opinion," De Masi told Euronews.
"Either way, it is imperative to create more transparency and remove stigma around the UAP issue and follow international efforts to create better reporting systems. This is not about green little men but the safety of our airspace and the vested interests of the military-industrial complex and national intelligence services," he added.
Reporting gap?
Despite several calls to include a standardised category for UAP reporting, the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) said it already provides a framework for reporting "any occurrence that may have an impact on aviation safety", including UAPs.
"Pilots and other aviation personnel are encouraged to report anything they consider to represent a potential safety risk, regardless of its nature," EASA told Euronews. The agency dismissed pilots' requests to designate a UAP-specific category, instead of a miscellaneous incidents category.
EASA assesses incidents based on available evidence and the potential impact on aviation safety, the agency said.
"At present, EASA has not identified evidence indicating that reports of UAP represent a systemic aviation safety issue requiring additional measures," it added.
However, some safety advocates suggest EASA's lack of evidence may stem from a reporting gap rather than an absence of events.
In the Netherlands, the Dutch Safety Board has stepped in to accept UAP reports from flight crews under a general category. Germany's Federal Aviation Office has also engaged in scientific research on the topic.
Without a standardised central database, advocates say, these localised insights remain fragmented, leaving the European agency with an incomplete picture of airspace anomalies.
Nuclear power plants
The plot thickens when UAPs are widely reported near nuclear facilities.
A 2015 French economic study confirmed that sightings of unexplained phenomena in France correlate with proximity to atomic sites. One such site is the La Hague reprocessing plant, where large quantities of highly radioactive materials are stored before and after reprocessing.
Similarly, incidents in the UK, such as the 1993 sightings over the Hartlepool nuclear power station and the infamous 1980 Rendlesham Forest incident near the RAF Bentwaters nuclear storage bunkers, have long fuelled public speculation.
UAP sightings have been associated with US nuclear facilities since the 1940s. Military personnel have reported unexplained objects near nuclear missile silos, weapons storage sites and nuclear power plants.
One of the most well-known cases occurred in 1967 at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, where former US Air Force officers claimed that a UAP was observed near missile silos just before several nuclear missiles became temporarily inoperable.
Similar incidents have been reported at other military installations, including Minot Air Force Base and sites in the southwestern United States.
While many witnesses consider these events significant, no conclusive evidence has been found to establish the origin or nature of the objects involved. The US government is currently investigating UAP reports, but the causes of these incidents remain unresolved.
The paradox of boosting defence capabilities
The EU is currently asking EU countries to increase defence spending, cooperate more closely and invest jointly in European defence capabilities under the bloc's binding industrial and military targets to ensure Europe is defence-ready by the end of the decade.
But when it comes to UAPs, Brussels argues this must be monitored at the national level.
Euronews asked the Commission whether it was considering any information-sharing mechanism between the US and the EU regarding UAPs, or whether it intended to act on its own to monitor and assess them, taking into account possible impacts on flight safety.
"UAP are the responsibility of EU member states, which handle them according to national security and defence priorities," a Commission spokesperson responded.
Akkermans urged the EU to treat UAPs as an aviation safety reality rather than a taboo.
"We need the EASA, the European Commission and the Parliament to formally update our aviation safety frameworks with a standardised UAP reporting category, ending the policy of ignoring or misclassifying data. Right now, the system is forcing us to stay silent," the Dutch pilot said.
For van Heijst, it is crucial to "get rid of the stigma" around the UAP topic since "there is a genuine concern for flight safety".
"This is highlighted by the swarms of (potentially Russian military) drones that invaded European airspace en masse last year. Ignoring these things is in complete contradiction to the high standards of aviation safety in the EU," van Heijst said.

Qantas A380 flew to US and back with maintenance light left in wing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:04:52 UTC
17:04:52 KST

ATSB investigation finds maintenance light was left in Qantas A380 jet wing
In short:
A work light was left inside the wing of a Qantas A380, which flew multiple international trips before it was found.
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said it was due to a breakdown in processes at Qantas.
What's next?
Qantas has established a working group and changed its tool-control procedures.
A Qantas A380 was cleared to fly passengers return from Sydney to Dallas with a large maintenance light accidentally left inside its wing.
It follows a 2023 incident in which a large tool was left inside a Qantas A380 engine and was not recovered until multiple international trips had been completed.
An Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation found the 33 centimetre light was left behind after maintenance on the aircraft's air conditioning system in Sydney on January 7.
The aircraft then flew to Dallas-Fort Worth and back before maintenance staff realised the light was missing and recovered it from the wing two days later.
The ATSB's final report into the incident found that although the light did not cause any damage to the wing, foreign objects posed a "significant risk to the safe operation of an aircraft".
ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said the incident was due to a breakdown in tool accountability processes.
"Even well-established processes can be vulnerable when they rely solely on consistent human performance, particularly during maintenance tasks which are often conducted in challenging environments and under operational pressures," he said.
"Tool control systems and procedures must account for this variability with safeguards to detect and recover from errors."
The report said Qantas issued a safety directive to address changes to its tooling control processes and procedures and had also formed a "tooling working group".
Qantas said the light had no impact on the operation of the aircraft and it had voluntarily reported the incident to the ATSB.
"Since the event, we have strengthened our tool-control procedures, including introducing a mandatory pre-clearance check to confirm all tooling is accounted for following maintenance," a spokesperson said.
Second tool left inside Qantas A380
It is the second incident involving a tool being left in one of the airline's super jumbos.
In December 2023, a Qantas A380 flew multiple international trips before a 1.25 metre nylon turning tool was discovered in one of the plane's engines.
An ATSB report found maintenance staff "lost" the "turning tool" in an A380's outboard engine, and it was only discovered after it had been cleared for service, flying multiple trips between Australia and the US.
Last week, Qantas passengers in South Africa were left stranded in Johannesberg for three days after a problem with the nose wheel of an A380 saw their flight to Sydney cancelled.
Qantas sent another flight to bring the stranded passengers home.
CQUniversity aviation expert and associate professor Steven Leib said any unaccounted-for objects found inside an aircraft were "a real safety concern".
"It may not seem like a big deal, leaving a light or leaving a tool, but these are things that could move around during flight, which could jeopardise the safety of the flight," Dr Leib said.
However, he said the two incidents were not enough to suggest Qantas had a systemic problem.
"The discovery of the lost object was made by the accountability system," he said.
"They were able to trace when it was last used, when it was meant to have been returned and what work was being carried out."

Taichung partners with RAI Technology on smart traffic management

08:02:24 UTC
17:02:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung announced Monday that it has partnered with RAI Technology to deploy an AI-backed traffic monitoring system in busy areas, according to a city Transportation Bureau press release.
The Transportation Bureau signed a memorandum of understanding with RAI. The bureau said this marks a transition to active detection, real-time notification, and data-backed decision-making.
Transportation Bureau Director Yeh Chao-fu (葉昭甫) said the new system will reduce staff workload, as monitoring was previously done manually to verify accidents and traffic congestion. He noted that going through surveillance footage causes delays as responders await confirmation.
Yeh said the bureau will prioritize the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi-Far Eastern Department Stores shopping area in the Seventh Redevelopment Zone, with AI monitoring along Taiwan Boulevard, Huizhong Road, and Shizheng North 7th Road tracking vehicles near parking lots. When vehicle queues reach a preset threshold, the system will generate a detailed report and notify traffic management staff to determine the appropriate response.
Yeh said the city will then target the entry and exit ramps of Provincial Highway 74 by using cameras at Huanzhong East Road and Taiyuan Road to assess traffic flow. The bureau will use collected statistics to determine the appropriate traffic control measures.
Yeh said the third pilot will take place during the Xinshe Flower Festival, where cameras will be set up at shuttle bus terminals. Once the queue reaches a preset threshold, the system will notify the bureau to respond accordingly.

Taiwan personnel agency rejects proposal to scrap National Travel Card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:02:00 UTC
17:02:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet's personnel administration rejected a proposal to end the National Travel Card program, saying it encourages civil servants to take annual leave and protects employee health, CNA reported Monday.
UDN reported that the proposal was posted on the government's Public Policy Network Participation Platform. It called for ending the card program and allowing unused leave to be fully compensated in cash when civil servants cannot take time off because of work demands.
The proposal said the current system requires part of the compensation linked to unused leave to be spent through the National Travel Card. It argued that restrictions on eligible purchases limit how civil servants can use the money.
In response, the personnel administration said it would not adopt the proposal for now. It said replacing the system with cash payments could give civil servants less incentive to take enough time off, per Up Media.
The agency said required leave days help protect employees' physical and mental health. Government figures show civil servants took an average of 11.32 days of annual leave in 2025.
Civil servants entitled to more than 10 days of annual leave are generally required to take at least 10 days. They can receive up to NT$16,000 (US$502) a year through the National Travel Card program, per Liberty Times.
Half of the subsidy can be spent without tourism-related restrictions. The other NT$8,000 must be used for tourism-related spending.
The personnel administration said the card subsidy is a welfare benefit rather than overtime pay or direct compensation for unused leave. Civil servants who cannot use all their annual leave because of work demands can still claim cash compensation for up to 20 unused days beyond the required 10 days.
The Cabinet has approved keeping the current rules from 2026 through 2028. The personnel administration said the program is generally reviewed every three years, per FTV News.
The National Travel Card program began in 2003 to encourage civil servants to take vacations and support domestic tourism. Critics say the program has since moved away from its original purpose.
Former Minister without Portfolio Chang Ching-sen (張景森), opposition lawmakers, and civil servant groups have called for changes to the system. Their proposals include easing spending restrictions, raising the subsidy, or replacing the card with cash payments.
Some civil servants also question whether the card still encourages tourism. They say the subsidy is often spent on hotel vouchers, meals, or everyday goods instead.

China’s passport warfare targets Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-17
08:01:57 UTC
17:01:57 KST

China is turning travel documents, overflight permits, visas, and border checkpoints into weapons in a quiet campaign to isolate Taiwan from the world.
In late April, Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar revoked overflight clearances for President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) planned flight to Eswatini under pressure from Beijing. Taipei and Mbabane outmaneuvered the blockade when King Mswati III’s aircraft transported the Taiwanese delegation on a much longer route through friendly airspace, landing safely in Eswatini on May 2.
By July, this containment campaign had begun targeting ordinary citizens. The Moroccan Embassy in Tokyo halted mandatory visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese tourists, forcing Taipei to respond with a reciprocal visa suspension against Moroccan nationals.
In August, Ugandan immigration officers at Entebbe International Airport withheld Taiwanese passports and demanded that Taiwanese travelers produce Chinese passports before their documents would be returned.
These shocks reveal a trend toward “passport warfare” — the weaponization of airspace, transit hubs, visas, and checkpoints to isolate Taiwan. This administrative containment mirrors the coercive diplomatic warfare the Chinese Communist Party aggressively conducts against countries that maintain official relations with Taiwan.
By forcing foreign states to deny transit, entry, or basic document recognition to Taiwanese passport holders, Beijing achieves through bureaucratic pressure what it cannot yet enforce through military might. The result directly undermines cross-strait deterrence and assurance.
The Zero-Tariff Cauldron
These travel restrictions reflect clear geopolitical patterns.
Sovereignty fears drive complete transit blockades in Georgia and Moldova, where governments fear legitimizing breakaway regions and have strong reasons to please Beijing. Economic dependencies dictate entry bans in Venezuela and Azerbaijan, while Chinese investment in Morocco’s Tangier Tech Smart City forms part of the broader context for Rabat’s recent visa freeze.
Elsewhere, proxy disputes dictate borders, as Somalia has barred Taiwanese travelers in retaliation for Taipei’s ties with Somaliland.
This African containment stems from a unified economic carrot. On Feb. 14, during the 39th African Union Summit, Chinese leader Xi Jinping announced a unilateral zero-tariff policy for 53 African nations, effective May 1.
Eswatini, Taiwan’s only diplomatic ally in Africa, was the sole African country excluded from Beijing’s duty-free umbrella.
In exchange, African leaders have increasingly aligned their borders and diplomatic language with Beijing. Recent joint declarations with hardline dependents such as Zimbabwe, Equatorial Guinea, Algeria, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have dropped historical language endorsing a peaceful resolution of cross-strait relations.
By stating only that Taiwan is an inalienable part of Chinese territory and omitting references to peace, these accords grant diplomatic cover to a future military blockade.
Deterrence, Assurance, and Silkworms
International relations theory holds that deterrence relies on raising the costs of aggression, while assurance guarantees that maintaining the status quo preserves security.
Beijing’s passport warfare subverts this balance through consular and airspace deterrence. It creates a gray-zone barrier to prove that standard travel can result in immediate logistical stranding.
This behavior embodies the Chinese idiom 蠶食鯨吞, or “to nibble away like a silkworm before swallowing like a whale.”
Avoiding hot war, Beijing relies on the silkworm’s patience. It pressures civil aviation systems, border authorities, and travel-document databases to make Taiwanese mobility appear abnormal, disputed, and administratively inconvenient.
Squeezing access in isolated hubs gradually conditions the world to accept Taiwan’s isolation. Once this erasure is normalized, the strategy can shift to the whale’s swallow: collapsing status quo assurances and eliminating Taiwan’s international presence entirely.
The Expanding Gray-Zone Grid
This containment has expanded beyond historic non-recognition blocks, combining passport warfare and legal pressure into a unified lawfare campaign.
In South Africa, Pretoria excluded Taiwan from its automated e-visa platform and demanded that Taiwan move its liaison office from Pretoria to Johannesburg, treating travel access and representation as concessions to Beijing.
In China’s own legal system, the CCP has expanded extraterritorial threats. Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has raised concerns over Article 63 of China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which targets overseas organizations and individuals accused of undermining ethnic unity or promoting separatism.
At the same time, Chinese judicial guidelines on “Taiwan independence” have turned travel through China and China-aligned states into a growing risk for Taiwanese, overseas Taiwanese, and foreign supporters of Taiwan.
Thailand and South Korea have also intensified screening of Taiwanese arrivals under the pretext of fighting transnational fraud, demonstrating how ordinary border enforcement can be turned into broader friction against Taiwanese mobility.
Uganda’s August passport seizures show the campaign’s most blunt form. Ugandan immigration officers at Entebbe withheld Taiwanese passports, demanded Chinese passports, and in earlier cases detained or deported Taiwanese travelers.
Foreign nationals are not immune. Western and other foreign passport holders who renew documents through trade offices or de facto embassies in Taipei can face denial or heightened scrutiny at Chinese checkpoints when “Taipei” appears as the place of issue. In China’s political reading of travel documents, even a neutral administrative field can become a sovereignty trap.
The same pattern appears in paperwork erasure. Serbia and Bolivia process visas for Taiwanese on loose sheets of paper, while Jamaica requires travelers to purchase a separate affidavit of identity to avoid creating an official administrative record on a Taiwanese passport.
The September Entry and Exit Codes
The structural normalization of passport warfare is arriving through China’s sweeping new entry and exit regulation, State Council Decree No. 841, which takes effect Sept. 15.
The 19-article regulation gives Beijing broader administrative tools to refuse entry, cancel transit, restrict exit, demand supporting documents, require electronic data, and impose entry bans on people accused of violating vague border or national-security classifications.
This codifies a weapon-ready architecture for gray-zone border control.
Under the new regulation, border officers and visa authorities can demand documents, materials, and electronic data when verifying a traveler’s identity or stated purpose of travel. False materials or statements can be used to deny entry or exit documents, refuse entry, or impose bans of one to five years.
The system gives Beijing more tools to punish travelers whose identities, documents, political views, or links to Taiwan are deemed irregular.
Because Beijing routinely treats Taiwanese as Chinese citizens under its domestic administrative practices, these measures could be selectively applied to Taiwanese tech workers, academics, businesspeople, activists, and public figures traveling to or from China.
What appears to be a border-management rule is in practice another tool for ideological compliance.
The Democratic Counterstrike
To neutralize this strategy, Taiwan and its allies must establish diplomatic counter-deterrence.
First, democratic partners should impose immediate diplomatic costs on states that target Taiwanese travelers. Taiwan’s July 30 reciprocal visa suspension against Morocco offers a model.
If a state bans Taiwanese transit, withholds passports, or enforces discriminatory entry rules under Beijing’s pressure, the US, EU, Japan, Canada, Australia, and other partners should respond with bureaucratic delays, reciprocal scrutiny, or restrictions on electronic visa access for that country’s officials.
Second, allies must mobilize multilateral aviation protections.
Beijing’s airspace coercion violates the apolitical spirit of the Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation. Western allies should explicitly extend freedom-of-navigation principles to civil aviation by guaranteeing alternative routes, priority transit, diplomatic escorts, or emergency logistical support for Taiwanese officials facing blockade attempts.
Eswatini’s royal-jet intervention showed that Beijing’s airspace choke points can be broken. The democratic world should systematize that lesson before the next attempted blockade.
Third, allies should establish pre-cleared sovereign whitelisting.
The US, Canada, UK, and Schengen Area should integrate Taiwan into automated, depoliticized biometric corridors such as Global Entry, SmartGate, and similar trusted-traveler systems. Bypassing manual embassy checks protects travelers from localized diplomatic pressure.
This automation is urgent. As the Uganda passport seizures show, Taiwan often lacks local embassies and must route emergency support through remote offices, such as its representative office in Somaliland.
Automated and trusted systems would make Taiwan’s global mobility harder to break, even under China’s incoming Sept. 15 border rules.
A Global Blueprint for Erasure
Passport warfare is an existential threat disguised as paperwork.
The institutional foundations for this global containment were codified during the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation meeting in Beijing, where every participating African head of state except Eswatini declared support for China’s “national reunification” narrative and “all efforts by the Chinese government” to achieve the goal.
Driven by Beijing’s economic leverage, this language fuels the silkworm’s first nibble, expanding the blockade into a systemic global consular net.
In Southeast Asia, staunch Beijing allies such as Cambodia and Laos have weaponized visa infrastructure by tightening restrictions on Taiwanese nationals while offering broader entry privileges to Chinese citizens.
In South America, China has used expanded visa-waiver frameworks with core trade partners such as Brazil, Argentina, and Peru to encourage compliance with Beijing’s passport and sovereignty demands, increasingly choking off standard entry procedures for Taiwanese travelers.
Normalizing a world where autocrats dictate international transit does not prevent conflict. It accelerates the whale’s final swallow.
If the democratic world fails to break Beijing’s consular blockade today, its own freedom of movement will be held hostage tomorrow.
